items.title: As it happened: Late crash sees Dutch dominance continue in women's UCI Gravel World Championships on muddy course
items.author: Tim Bonville-Ginn
items.content:
Marianne Vos went solo over the top of the final climb with Rosa Klöser crashing as she tried to follow. Larissa Hartop outsprinted Nele Laing to take bronze.

1. Marianne Vos (NED) 4:30'04"2. Rosa Klöser (GER) +27"

3. Larissa Hartog (NED) +2'15"

4. Nele Laing (GER) S.T.

5. Erica Magnaldi (ITA) +4'17"

6. Sofía Gómez Villafañe (ARG) +5'15"

7. Irina Lützelschwab (SWI) +5'28"

8. Tiffany Cromwell (AUS) +7'15"

9. Elisa Serné (NED) S.T.

10. Haley Smith (CAN) +8'55"

The temperatures have been high for much of the week but it is a cool and fresh 16°C, unusually low for spring time in the area.

October 9, 2026 – 9:24 PM

Hello and welcome to ' live updates of the women's UCI World Gravel Championships 2026 from Nannup, Western Australia.

October 9, 2026 – 9:28 PM

Info from our Australia Editor Simone Giuliani on the ground is that the course has had some overnight rain, compacting the pea gravel making the route less slippery.

However, the riders will have to contend with puddles, likely not to the same extent seen at Unbound this year, but still an extra challenge for the riders.

October 9, 2026 – 9:35 PM

The women face a challenging but rather short 125.6km of racing on the gravel of Western Australia, what should they be looking out for? Well, we've put together what we think will be the three things that could shape the racing...

October 9, 2026 – 9:39 PM

Racing is due to begin at 10:10 local time in Nannup. Roughly 30 minutes from now.

October 9, 2026 – 9:48 PM

For those who may not be familiar with the gravel scene but knows road will have one name screaming out at them, that being former world gravel champion Marianne Vos. However, there are some star specialists are here with Argentina's Sofia Gomez Villafañe, home rider Nicole Frain and many more all lining up to challenge.

October 9, 2026 – 9:53 PM

The course itself is extremely challenging. While it is rather short, in the 125.6km of racing there are 3180 metres of elevation gain with the climbs not allow immediate rest after the summits are they tend to plateau for a while afterwards.

October 9, 2026 – 9:55 PM

The gravel is like nothing seen in European gravel racing and is unique to the area in Australia. Pea gravel is what it says on the tin, gravel that is shaped like peas. It can been incredibly slippery when dry but when wet it can be compacted down and become less notable with tyre choice being crucial.

October 9, 2026 – 9:58 PM

The riders are beginning to line up on the start line in Nannup with Wendy Oosterwoud of the Netherlands wearing number one.

October 9, 2026 – 10:04 PM

It is being said that this is a 'true' gravel course with 85% of the course on gravel with intense gradients and a huge amount of climbing. The chance for the specialists to finally have a pure gravel rider in the rainbow bands after road stars have dominated the first four editions.

October 9, 2026 – 10:06 PM

This will be the final race in the career of South African WorldTour rider Ashleigh Moolman-Pasio despite having a cold.

October 9, 2026 – 10:08 PM

Australian gravel champion and winner here for the SEVEN Gravel race in Nannup earlier in the year, Tiffany Cromwell, is another rider who will be hanging up the wheels after this race.

October 9, 2026 – 10:10 PM

Racing begins for the 2026 Gravel World Championships in Nannup with the Dutch team immediately up to the front.

October 9, 2026 – 10:13 PM

It is a fast start on the asphalt to begin with the tiny peloton bunched together for the moment but when they hit the gravel it'll likely immediately split up.

October 9, 2026 – 10:18 PM

The home nation gets the ball rolling with the first attack of the day. No-one keen on following for the time being as we are still on the asphalt with 10km until the gravel begins.

October 9, 2026 – 10:19 PM

12 riders down as DNFs including Germany's Romy Kaspar and the Netherlands' Riejanne Markus.

October 9, 2026 – 10:23 PM

Bloor has a gap of just 12" on the peloton as the gravel edges closer and closer.

October 9, 2026 – 10:27 PM

Bloor leads onto the gravel with a very wet surface and a few puddles. A couple of early twitches from the back wheel for the Australian rider. She now has 34" on the peloton.

October 9, 2026 – 10:28 PM

The peloton hit the gravel and immediately things change as the pace shoots up with the Dutch crowding the front still. 5km to the first climb of the day.

October 9, 2026 – 10:30 PM

Bloor's wheel skipping and skidding all over the place forcing her to freewheel. All the riders have only been able to recon some of the route due to some of the sections being on private property including the first climb of the day.

October 9, 2026 – 10:32 PM

Mud is already caking the backs of the riders as the riders are on the first climb of the day now.

October 9, 2026 – 10:34 PM

Mutsumi Hara (Japan) and Elizabeth Hermolle (Great Britain) early off the back but it is a tough start and there's a long way to go as the rain begins to fall again.

October 9, 2026 – 10:40 PM

The gap goes out to a minute for Bloor who will be very happy for the moment but I imagine she would like to have some company. She rides solo for the time being.

October 9, 2026 – 10:40 PM

The climb Killarney which is 5.4km of very undulating riding and an average of 3.4% but with some nasty kickers.

October 9, 2026 – 10:43 PM

Multiple riders now struggling to hold onto the peloton as Bloor has 1'02" on the pack.

October 9, 2026 – 10:46 PM

One unexpected rider on the startlist for the elite women was Peta Mullens (Australia) who was expecting to ride the age group of 35-39 but received an email a few days ago saying she will have to race the elite due to rule changes coming into force...

October 9, 2026 – 10:46 PM

Bloor's gap has now reduced significantly as she continues to tap out a rhythm that suits her but she now just has 30" on the chasers.

October 9, 2026 – 10:47 PM

The peloton has shrunk quite a lot on this first climb with Bloor being reeled back in very soon.

October 9, 2026 – 10:50 PM

Former Australian national road champion Nicole Frain is keen to see a gravel specialist take the title today...

October 9, 2026 – 10:52 PM

Not ideal for the Irish rider who clipped a wheel and came down. She is back riding but is now out of the back.

October 9, 2026 – 10:53 PM

Inside 1km from the top of the Killarney climb as Bloor holds a very slender lead.

October 9, 2026 – 10:55 PM

Bloor is caught by the Dutch led peloton that has been whittled right down on the first climb.

October 9, 2026 – 10:56 PM

Onto the first descent of the day now and the pace shot up to make sure they were in a good position with Vos, Sophie Wright (Great Britain) and Larissa Hartog (Netherlands) leading the way.

October 9, 2026 – 10:57 PM

The sun is back out now but the gravel is very wet and slippy.

October 9, 2026 – 10:59 PM

One of the big favourites for the race is trying to fix this quickly with her plugs but the sealant taking a while. She is now back riding but a long way out the back now. Similar happened in Unbound earlier this year.

October 9, 2026 – 11:00 PM

Some info coming from the start... The age groupers are heading out in waves now. Some were so keen to ensure a good spot in the start line that they were sitting in the ground with their bikes in their start box well over an hour before their start time.

October 9, 2026 – 11:03 PM

Maddy Nutt (Great Britain) was just off the back after that descent but has made it back in now. She will be relying on her huge engine and stamina to be involved in the final...

October 9, 2026 – 11:05 PM

The peloton now bunches up after that descent as they build towards the first majorly hard climb of Brockwell.

October 9, 2026 – 11:05 PM

Wright, Hartog, Cromwell and Erica Magnaldi (Italy) lead the peloton on this rolling terrain.

October 9, 2026 – 11:09 PM

Onto the Brockman climb with Wright and Magnaldi upping the tempo with the rain starting yet again. You won't win the race here but you can certainly lose it.

October 9, 2026 – 11:10 PM

The climb is 2.5km at 8% with kicks well over 15%.

October 9, 2026 – 11:11 PM

Klöser has fought very well and is about 10" off the back of the lead group and is picking up riders who are losing touch.

October 9, 2026 – 11:13 PM

Wright is ripping this peloton to bits on this climb but Klöser is about to make it back on.

October 9, 2026 – 11:14 PM

Klöser flies pass British duo of Nutt and Hermolle as they have to negotiate their way around one of the camera bikes that has got stuck in the mud on the gradients of Brockman.

October 9, 2026 – 11:15 PM

Wendy Oosterwoud (Netherlands), Gravel World Series leader, has been gapped just before the hardest section. That is a big surprise.

October 9, 2026 – 11:16 PM

Cromwell also out of the back with Denmark's Janni Spangsberg Schori losing tough as well.

October 9, 2026 – 11:17 PM

The Dutch still just about have four riders in this select group with Hartog and Geerike Schreurs just holding on.

October 9, 2026 – 11:21 PM

Sofía Gómez Villafañe (Argentina)Nicole Frain (Australia)

Marianne Vos (Netherlands)

Ashleigh Moolman-Pasio (South Africa) Erica Magnaldi (Italy)

Elisa Serné (Netherlands)

Rosa Klöser (Germany)

Geerike Schreurs (Netherlands)

Larissa Hartog (Netherlanda)

Irina Lützelschwab (Switzerland)

Haley Smith (Canada)

And a few others now lead.

October 9, 2026 – 11:21 PM

Wright did all that work on the toughest gradients but has not made the group.

October 9, 2026 – 11:22 PM

Cromwell, Wright, Oosterwoud are now around 45" down on the leaders.

October 9, 2026 – 11:23 PM

Through the feed zone now as multiple riders take on fresh bottles, bars and gels.

October 9, 2026 – 11:24 PM

Great crowds around the feed area after a period on private land.

October 9, 2026 – 11:24 PM

On the Adina climb now, 1.1km long at 4% average.

October 9, 2026 – 11:27 PM

Bit of grass racing turns into mud and then some more traditional looking gravel for a very short period before returning back to the pea gravel very soon.

October 9, 2026 – 11:30 PM

She has a front flat but she seems to have got it fixed pretty fast.

October 9, 2026 – 11:35 PM

The gap between the lead group including Vos, Villafañe, Klöser, Moolman-Pasio and the rest have a minute on the group including Cromwell, Wright and Oosterwoud.

October 9, 2026 – 11:37 PM

Onto Shale climb of 800m at 6.8% which is being done very swiftly as Villafañe and Magnaldi lead the way for now.

October 9, 2026 – 11:42 PM

The Shale climb appears to have favoured the chase group as the gap drops to 22", but this will be based on the motorbikes so we take that gap with a pinch of salt.

October 9, 2026 – 11:43 PM

And the gap is closing. 15" between the leaders and chasers as riders like Cromwell, Oosterwoud and Flora Johnson (Great Britain) may get back in.

October 9, 2026 – 11:45 PM

Cromwell is leading the chasing group back to the front group as the leader's pace lulls. That was a big effort from the chasers with Oosterwoud still struggling to hold the wheel but we now have a lead group of around 16 riders.

October 9, 2026 – 11:47 PM

Tiffany Cromwell (Australia)

The Australian champion launches as soon as she re-joined the leaders to try and get clear but she is solo and the chase is on.

October 9, 2026 – 11:50 PM

Vos tried a move but she was heavily marked. Cromwell continues to press on as the chase group starts to sit up a bit more.

October 9, 2026 – 11:52 PM

Magnaldi is investing a lot of energy on the front of the favourites group without dropping anyone but they stall again and allow Cromwell a bit more gap.

October 9, 2026 – 11:53 PM

Cromwell expands her lead to 10" as the chase stalls.

October 9, 2026 – 11:54 PM

Marianne Vos (Netherlands)

The former world champion launches for a second time to try and close Cromwell down. She is marked but it has got the rest of the group interested in chasing again.

October 9, 2026 – 11:55 PM

Cromwell heads onto the descent, probably the longest downhill of the entire race.

October 9, 2026 – 11:59 PM

Vos came into this race with an eye on the gravel specialists as the superstar hopes to become the first rider to take a second gravel world title...

October 10, 2026 – 12:00 AM

Cromwell drags her advantage out to 19" and is now out of sight from the chase group as the Aussie goes solo in the Worlds, on home soil, in her final race.

October 10, 2026 – 12:06 AM

Geerike Schreurs (Netherlands)Ashleigh Moolman-Pasio (South Africa)

The latter gets back on her feet but isn't in a rush to get going while Schreurs stays on the ground with the medics tending to both.

October 10, 2026 – 12:07 AM

There was a very nasty rut that they hit and it just pushed Schreurs and Moolman-Pasio out with the former kicked to the side and into the rocks. Both look to be out of the race.

October 10, 2026 – 12:08 AM

Meanwhile, Cromwell has 27" gap on the chase group.

October 10, 2026 – 12:11 AM

A brief section of asphalt heads back onto the gravel and Cromwell has 48" on the chasers.

October 10, 2026 – 12:16 AM

The Dutch have numbers but are not chasing with the Germans taking the responsibility through a very rocky and puddle filled section as Cromwell opens her gap to 1'17".

October 10, 2026 – 12:18 AM

Now time for the Lewana climb, 1.5km at 5.3%.

October 10, 2026 – 12:19 AM

A stick has got into her rear mech. She is back riding but another issue for the German after an earlier puncture.

items.title: 'I'm kind of nervous' – Will mystery knee injury hold Isaac del Toro back at Il Lombardia?
items.author: Patrick Fletcher
items.content:
In the eyes of many, Isaac del Toro is the favourite for Il Lombardia, but there is a question mark hanging over the Mexican, in the form of a mysterious knee injury.

Del Toro first revealed the issue ahead of Gran Piemonte on Thursday, and though he did go on to ride an aggressive race, he has highlighted the issue on numerous occasions since, both after the race and again on Friday, on the eve of Il Lombardia.

"It's going ok, I think today I've had no real discomfort. I don't know what might happen, but I'm hoping it'll be ok tomorrow," Del Toro said at the teams presentation in Bergamo the evening before the 'race of the falling leaves'.

"We're dealing with the necessary things: feeling good and finishing off the year well.

Del Toro hasn't been able to pinpoint the specific cause of the pain.

"I don't know why. After the travel I started to have some trouble," he'd said ahead of Gran Piemonte. "I had the same bikes, same shoes, same everything. I don’t know."

On Friday, he revealed that he feels the pain mostly when he's riding in the saddle.

Del Toro, who has had an extraordinary third professional season with a Tour de France podium and three WorldTour stage race titles, has a huge opportunity to land a first Monument of his career.

With Tadej Pogačar absent, and having placed fifth behind his all-conquering teammate here 12 months ago, Del Toro faces the likes of Remco Evenepoel and Paul Seixas but has a clear shot at glory in Como on Saturday – if of course the knee holds up.

"It’s normal we want to finish it off in Il Lombardia, we want to do it better," he said.

"It’s not a secret I had this kind of problem. We need to be high with the mentality and also do super good.

"I don't know, I'm kind of nervous,. But if the body is going good, I’m happy."

items.title: Young USCX champion Tofik Beshir in ICU at Tennessee hospital after 'head-on crash' on gravel ride
items.author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
items.content:
Young cyclo-cross star Tofik Beshir (CXD Trek Bikes) was involved in a "head-on crash" while riding his bike on a gravel road Thursday in the vicinity of Lees-McRae College in western North Carolina and is currently in intensive care.

It is unclear at present what the nature of the collision was, or whether a vehicle was involved.

He was taken to the hospital in Johnson City, Tennessee, where he remains in the ICU.

According to a GoFundMe page, the 19-year-old sustained "injuries consistent with brain shear trauma". His parents were with him.

"He is not conscious yet, and there are still a lot of unknowns. Healing thoughts and prayers are what he needs right now. I will update his status as we learn more," the statement read on the crowdfunding page.

Beshir grew up in Arlington, Virginia, his parents both from Ethiopia. This fall, he moved to Banner Elk, North Carolina, where he is a freshman at Lees-McRae College and competes as a multi-discipline rider on their cycling team.

He competed in the elite races at the US Cyclocross Series in September and early October, where he won five of the six races, two of them C1, and secured the USCX series title.

As of Saturday morning, the GoFundMe page had raised $49,988 with a goal of $200,000 to help fund Beshir's medical care.

"We are asking for donations to help fund Tofik and his family's medical care on his long road to recovery. Expenses may include time in the ICU, longterm stay in the hospital, PT, family expenses as they stay near Johnson City, and anything else that may arise," the fundraising page read.

items.title: Brandon McNulty: I don't feel burdened by the rainbow jersey, I just feel like I'm trying to honour it
items.author: Patrick Fletcher
items.content:
Brandon McNulty is getting used to the feel of those rainbows around his chest. He’s already had four outings in the world champion’s jersey in the 12 days since his stunning victory in Montreal, and it’s fair to say he’s given it a good airing.

Riding Giro dell’Emilia, Coppa Agostoni, Tre Valli Varesine, and Gran Piemonte in the last few days, he has been a spritely presence, animating each race with a series of attacks.

“It’s been super special,” McNulty told the gathered media at the teams presentation in Bergamo the evening before Il Lombardia.

“Obviously I’m still the same rider. It’s not like I’m all of a sudden better, but it’s just nice to race with a bit of confidence, just to attack and whatnot, it’s been really nice.”

McNulty highlighted out a caveat when it comes to his racing style in recent days. These late-season Italian Classics are, he argued, “always a bit more open and free”. And then there’s the small matter of Tadej Pogačar’s injury-enforced absence, which has not only opened most of these races up to the peloton as a whole but also in terms of the pecking order at UAE Team Emirates-XRG.

But it seems that the rainbow jersey, which can weigh heavily on some shoulders, is sitting rather lightly on his.

“I don’t really feel burdened by the jersey or anything. I just feel like I’m trying to honour it and just race aggressively.

“I think it does come with a bit of respect, or space [in the peloton],” he added, “but as I said these races are always a bit more relaxed already, so it might also just be that it’s the end of the year. I guess we’ll see tomorrow in a Monument how it will be.”

For all his racing freedom in recent days, McNulty did give the first indication that this rainbow jersey will be deployed on domestique duty.

“When we have a leader like Isaac [Del Toro] here it changes a bit the tactics,” McNulty said.

That idea of a world-champion helper hasn’t sat comfortably with some pundits, and while it will be a pretty obvious scenario when Pogačar is back next year, he confirmed the hierarchy has been set in a similar way for Il Lombardia.

“For sure he’ll be, like always, our first rider, but we always try to race aggressively with myself, so we’ll see, but the first thing is Isaac, for sure."

items.title: Lucinda Brand ready for 'exciting new chapter' on the road as she announces Lidl-Trek departure in wake of Luca Guercilena's exit
items.author: Owen Rogers
items.content:
At the same time, the world cyclo-cross champion has extended her winter contract with Baloise-Het Poetsbureau Lions, continuing her collaboration with team manager Sven Nys for two more seasons.

"When I was losing my joy for cycling, Sven brought it back. His passion, energy and belief in me made me fall in love with the sport all over again," she wrote.

"His dream? To become cyclocross world champions together. Sven also knew how much road cycling meant to me and made sure I could sign with Trek-Segafredo."

Since then, Brand has won two rainbow jerseys in cyclo-cross, among her 77 victories for Nys' team. At the same time, she refound her winning form on the road, winning her first race since 2017 in 2021, her second season with Lidl-Trek. She's followed that with 10 more in the ensuing seasons, including the Tour de Suisse, Thüringen Ladies Tour, and the Baloise Ladies Tour.

"I’ll always be grateful for the people and memories we shared. But sometimes life brings you to a crossroads," she wrote of her time with the team.

"Lidl-Trek offered me the chance to continue together, but it came with a difficult choice. To stay, I would have to leave behind the man who believed in me when I needed it most. The man who brought back my love for cycling and helped me become the rider I am today.

"And for me, that was never really a choice. Some things in life are bigger than results, contracts or opportunities. Loyalty. Trust. Family."

Brand concluded her post by announcing that she'll stay with Nys and Baloise-Het Poetsbureau Lions for two more years. Starting her 2026-27 season this weekend, at the HG Cross Dendermonde, she'll hope to continue the success of last season, where she won 20 races, including the world title, the UCI World Cup and X2O Badkamers Trofee titles.

Brand's road season ended in August, but she'll return next season for a different team, having ended her seven-year stint at Lidl-Trek. She'll announce her new road team next week.

"So today, I’m incredibly proud and happy to announce that I’ll continue racing for Baloise-Het Poetsbureau for the next two seasons!" she wrote.

"This means saying goodbye to Lidl-Trek. A chapter I’ll always look back on with a big smile and so much gratitude.

"But don’t worry, my road cycling story is far from over. An exciting new chapter is about to begin. Where will I be racing on the road? I’ll tell you next week!

"Some decisions are made with your head. Others are made with your heart. This one was never in doubt."

items.title: Primož Roglič says 'it's possible' Il Lombardia will be the final race of his career
items.author: Patrick Fletcher
items.content:
Primož Roglič has revealed that his future is very much up in the air, stating that “it’s possible” that Saturday’s Il Lombardia will be the final race of his decorated career.

The five-time Grand Tour winner, who turns 37 later this month, is coming to the end of his three-year spell at Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe, and while he has been linked with other teams, nothing has been decided as of yet.

Roglič indicated that he would prefer to race on into 2027, and suggested that’s the likely outcome, but behind the stage at the Il Lombardia team presentation in Bergamo on Friday evening he spoke surprisingly open-endedly about his future.

"You never know when is the last one," he said. "Like everything in life, it can be a bit emotional. I’m looking forward [to the race]."

Asked if he will continue to race next year, he said: "I don’t know it yet. We will see. We will see."

As for whether he wanted to, he replied: "I think so, yes. I think I will still race."

Roglič still needs to find and settle on a team, which is fairly unusual for someone of his stature at this point in the year. He has been linked with a number of teams since the summer, with Tudor Pro Cycling, Lotto-Intermarché, and Pinarello-Q36.5 all cited as possible destinations in recent reports from Daniel Benson’s Cycling Substack and .

But Roglič, curiously, left things open. Asked whether Lombardia might be the final race of his career, he said: "I think also possible yeah, you know, why not?

"We will see. I’m not worried. It’s life. We will see."

He then made an interesting comment that hinted at his motivation for carrying on in this sport, saying that had he won a fifth Vuelta a España title instead of finishing runner-up, he would be hanging up his wheels.

"You know, if I win the Vuelta for sure I would be out," he said. “But like this, it’s a bit…it’s still for me… you know… I want to finish it on a [high]."

As for his ability to go for those big results, the Vuelta and the end of the season have been something of a revelation for Roglič, who has endured a tough couple of seasons and looked to be a fading force.

But despite crashing ahead of the Vuelta and ruining his preparation, he finished runner-up and has gone on to light up the World Championships road race, finish 10th at the European road race, and earlier this week add to his palmarès with the European time trial title.

"It’s more difficult. It’s just more and more difficult to really find or do the right thing," Roglič said.

"The moment or the reality is I’m here; tomorrow I have a race. I have to do first things first, so first the racing and then I can speak about it and try to figure it out – when and how it can look, my future."

items.title: 'Mind-blowing' - Lachlan Morton's mid-point assessment of Pony Express endurance ride across 'very desolate landscapes' of US western states
items.author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
items.content:
Lachlan Morton passed the midway point Thursday on his latest long-distance challenge, the Pony Express route, camping for a few hours in Wyoming with rugged terrain populated by sagebrush and occasional cattle. Before his reprieve ahead on day four, riding through Utah's Emigration Canyon into Salt Lake City, the Australian gave an update to .

The ride so far, he said, was living up to expectations of "remote and harsh". He started on Monday in St. Joseph, Missouri, for the 3,164-kilometre (1,966-mile) ride across eight US western states into Sacramento, California. The route was made famous in the early 1860s by mail carriers racing on horseback. Morton is retracing the almost-exact path, using pedal power.

"I mean, there's just very desolate landscapes. They're all very different and challenging in their own way, but they're all very remote and harsh," he said in recorded answers to questions sent by of his first impressions of the route through Kansas, Nebraska, a touch into Colorado, and into Wyoming.

"I'm familiar with these landscapes, but then piecing them all together in this way, it's pretty mind-blowing."

At this point Morton was on the rough, almost-forgotten double-track leading from Wyoming to Salt Lake City. He had already encountered herds of cattle passing precariously close across his path and had a re-route through deep sand and leg-scratching brush under dark Wyoming skies when the almost-forgotten path seemed to vanish.

The original pioneers who raced across the open prairies and treacherous mountains switched their mounts several times to deliver papers and messages in eight days or less. The record on horseback was set in 1861 at seven days, 17 hours. Morton looks to beat that record, meeting up with support to switch bikes. It is a proper way for him to make his final ride in EF Education-EasyPost colours and equipment, where he has raced in multiple disciplines for 12 of the last 16 seasons.

"It's using all the different bikes I've ridden, and it's also very much a team effort. This is not something I could do by myself. It's relying on a group of people that I've come to know through my time with EF, and it's very much requiring a big effort by all of us, which I think has kind of been the story of my time with the team," he said.

The team posted to social media on Thursday that he was ahead of schedule, with a "400-kilometre lead over the Pony Express' fastest time" in Utah. However, the toughest terrain approached, and he admitted the opening days gave him a better understanding of the difficulty of the journey 160 years ago.

"I think it's a super interesting story for Pony Express, and the fact that it was around such a short time and is still, somehow, very celebrated and well known today," he said, referring to the two-year span of the Pony Express before the telegraph replaced the physical delivery of important messages.

"Seeing these landscapes and even trying to imagine doing it on horseback at all times in a year, night and day, it's pretty mind-blowing. I'm realising, I think, the power of the route."

On the weekend he'll cross Nevada, heading south of Lake Tahoe when he crosses the Sierra Nevada mountains that mark entry into California. In the true spirit of the route, Morton will deliver letters. It's all a flashback into history made real.

"It wasn't that there was heaps of people suddenly delivering mail. Ultimately, it didn't really work, it was never profitable. But the power of it was exciting. You know, it was something for people to be excited about at a time when the country was going through crazy change, and a lot of conflict. This was just a human-powered effort in a way that could get people excited about the country.

"That's kind of why I like to do these things. It's fun to do, but it's also nice to see people have something to follow for the sake of following and be excited about."

The names of the adventurous riders who blazed the first trails west are forever remembered on a Pony Express National Museum website. Perhaps Morton can make the list, with an asterisk. Follow Morton's progress online.

items.title: 'World Championships were just a snapshot' – Back to full confidence, Remco Evenepoel says victory at Il Lombardia would make 2026 his 'best season yet'
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
Six years after his horror crash at Il Lombardia, Remco Evenepoel (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe) is looking to close that chapter fully and cap off what would be "the best season of his career" with a maiden victory at the final Monument in 2026.

Speaking at a press conference on Friday, Evenepoel reportedly brought up the incident himself, which saw him crash over a bridge wall into a ravine on he steep descent off the Colma di Sormano.

While insisting it won't play on his mind during the race, especially as the climb is not included on this year's route to Como, Evenepoel did speak about how that crash will always make recons on the same roads in Lombardy special to him.

"It was good to check out the finale with the Civiglio, because I've never done that climb in a race before. In 2020 I didn't make it there because of that crash," he said, as reported by Flemish broadcaster .

"Because of the past, this race will always be special to me. During my reconnaissance, I passed by the hospital where I was treated 6 years ago [having fractured his pelvis and suffered a lung contusion in the crash].

"But none of that is on my mind. A victory could make it feel completely different, yes. Then we could wrap up the story and close the book. But it won't freeze me in this final."

Without five-time defending champion Tadej Pogačar taking the start, out injured, Evenepoel will start as one of the heavy favourites alongside Isaac del Toro (UAE Team Emirates-XRG), Paul Seixas (Decathlon CMA CGM), and Giulio Ciccone (Lidl-Trek). At 239km and with just under 5,000m of elevation gain, the Belgian believes the route should fit into his wheelhouse.

"It will be special with a difficult start featuring a few long climbs. Then follow two long valleys and short climbs at the end. So it seems like you get two races with an explosive finale at the end. That should suit me," he said, adding quiet confidence after identifying his main rivals.

"Seixas and Del Toro are obviously on fire, but there are more guys like Ciccone, Matteo Jorgenson and Tom Pidcock. Jarno Widar also looked good this week, but this is a different story altogether, with a lot of positioning work and many descents. That is something new for him.

"So you can't give very many guys 5 stars. If it can only be for one rider? Then go for me. But it will be an open race compared to previous years where the same rider won every time."

But after winning the European Championships road race last weekend, and with some reassurance from his entourage, the confidence has returned in time for the big appointment. He's been second at Lombardia twice, both behind Pogačar in 2025 and 2024, and will be desperate to go one better and add to his two Monument titles from Liège-Bastogne-Liège.

"After the World Championships, there was a sort of doubt as to whether I would get back into good form, but my trainer, team manager, and those back home reminded me that my World Championship time trial had still been super good," said Evenepoel.

"If you don't perform as you hope on the day of the appointment, you start to have some doubts. And you think: maybe it won't work out at the end of the year? But last Thursday I was able to train well towards the European Championships, and then I realized that the World Championships had been a snapshot.

"That European title gave me extra motivation. In any case, I can get over a disappointment quickly and refocus, but it certainly helped me."

In August last year, it was announced that Evenepoel would be breaking his Soudal-QuickStep contract early to join Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe in 2026. Fast forward to October, and with two stage wins and second overall at the Tour de France, victories at Amstel Gold Race, GP de Québec and Clasicá San Sebastián, podium finishes at Liège and the Tour of Flanders, and 13 wins in total, including a fourth consecutive ITT world title and the European road title, it's been nothing short of a major success.

"It's been pretty good. The classics campaign was pretty good, but I didn't necessarily reach the level I wanted. After Catalonia and my crash, it might have given a distorted picture, but I have been in better form in April," he said.

"Despite the good results, that was a somewhat weaker moment, but a strong summer followed. I have taken a step forward. Especially in the Grand Tours. That motivates us for the future.

"This is definitely one of my better seasons. If I win on Saturday, this will be my best season yet. Especially with my strong Tour. It would be a nice way to finish."

items.title: 'I would love to see an actual gravel rider winning the jersey' – An established gravel incarnation of Nicole Frain lines up as key hope for home-nation at Nannup Gravel World Championships
items.author: simone.giuliani@futurenet.com (Simone Giuliani)
items.content:
This is the third UCI Gravel World Championships for Australia's Nicole Frain, and she has been steadily working her way up the ranks, while also plotting out such a solid path in the discipline that it's easy to forget it's only her second season focused completely on gravel.

Back in 2024, when she first lined up at the rainbow jersey race, Frain had been racing on the road for Hess, though the team collapsed late in the season. However, she'd already been racing gravel at times in 2024, with strong results that included a run of seconds in RADL GRVL and the UCI Gravel World Series races of The Gralloch and Houffa and then her first World Championships in Belgium, where Marianne Vos won.

"I think the first year I definitely went in with no expectations, and then I surprised myself getting into a really good position. I had stomach issues, but at least for the race, I did put myself into a really good position if it all came together," said Frain who came over the line in 33rd.

Then in 2025 gravel became the main focus for the former Australian road champion, joining the Ridley team, throwing herself into the UCI Gravel World Series and honing her skills. Impressively she also took the overall victory at the series, which meant a start at the front of the field both packed with and dominated by Dutch riders.

"Last year, I learnt about the dynamic," Frain told in the weeks leading into the race. "In the Netherlands, it was not raced in your national federations. You looked around and you just saw all orange, and you realised all the helmets were also SD Worx, and it was very road rider dominated the last two years."

That second year she came 26th, but it's hard not to think that 2026 promises far more. On Saturday Frain will once again line up in the front section of the field, after taking second overall in the UCI Gravel World Series this year, but many other elements have changed.

For a start the race dynamics are expected to be wholly different his time. For a start, the shift for the first time outside Europe means there is no easy turnaround, and riders from other disciplines can't just drop in for a day, so there is less of a flood of European road professionals than in previous years. On top of that the nature of the course is completely different, heavy on climbing and gravel with more than 84% on the unpaved surfaces. This combination has made it a year where more and more key gravel specialists are turning up, raising the prospect that just maybe this year the road professional podium domination could come to an end.

"I would love to see an actual gravel rider winning the rainbow jersey, just because I think for the sport, seeing that at races will be really valuable," said Frain. "But yeah, of course, the best rider will win."

Just as the race situation has altered, so has Frain herself. Now into her second year as a full time gravel racer, having swapped over to Factor this year, and with an impressive list of wins right from claiming the Oceania Championships at RADL GRVL right at the start of the year to four UCI Gravel World Series race wins and also victory at the Unbound European qualifier of Heathland Gravel.

She has proven that she is a force to be reckoned with on gravel, so hopes are high that Frain could just be a rider who can show off the green and gold colours of the nation's jersey near the front at its home World Championships.

"It's definitely been one of my main targets," said Frain. "I've been putting a lot of the effort around that and prioritising everything into this period, so then it's always a little bit more personal pressure, I guess, because you know you put in a bit more effort here, and so you want to see a good outcome that you feel proud of as well."

There was some interruption to the preparation, with a bout of influenza stopping her in her tracks a couple of months ago, but having worked back from that it's now almost time to see what the results of that work and targeted focus will be.

"Generally it can suit me, if I'm having a good day," said Frain of the 125km course with 3,179m of elevation gain. "It does get more towards that heavy end of climbing for me, but then it's hard for everyone. So yeah, if I'm having a good day, and anybody that is smart about it can come away with a good result there, I think."

Though, no matter what you do in preparation gravel remains unpredictable and sometimes that's a blessing and other times its a curse.

"It's still gravel, and anything can happen. Puncture risk is higher and things like that," said Frain. "So you just try not to put too much emphasis on the race because you just want to be happy with whatever you put in.

"But at the same time, yes, it's super important and it is a good opportunity for me to get a nice result and that would ,of course, be the dream."

items.title: Can cyclists actually avoid injuries and illness? Experts examined three years of UAE Team Emirates-XRG data to find out
items.author: James Witts
items.content:
Less unusual is an unusual fact: “There are significantly more crashes on the right side than on the left. We can’t explain why. We’re looking into it.” The words of Raaghib Fredericks, UAE Team Emirates-XRG doctor, at this July’s Science & Cycling conference in Barcelona, where the South African presented his provisional findings on the injury and illness rates at the world’s leading cycling team for seasons 2019 to 2021. That crash bias was a footnote to a fascinating hour that revealed why staying injury- and illness-free is the most significant (albeit unsexy) performance boost a team and its riders can enjoy…

“What do we currently know about injuries and illness at WorldTour level?” asks Fredericks. “Very little. There have been nominal studies in this area, including terrific research entitled ‘ by a team led by Dr Thomas Fallon [of Queen’s University Belfast]. We set out to add to Fallon’s work.”

Fredericks’ research covered 30 male cyclists and analysed injury and illness data from the team’s cloud-based medical database, which was updated weekly. He could then compare those rates against training data from TrainingPeaks, the idea being that by pinning down injury and illness rates against factors like training loads, UAE Team Emirates-XRG could integrate protocols and best practice in search of, if not preventing and eliminating, at least ameliorating the impact of injuries and illness, which are significant. “Over the three seasons analysed, we lost 1,920 racing and training days to illness and injury,” he says. “That equates to around two lost days per rider each month.”

That absence varied from one day to months, as in the case of Diego Ulissi, who the team announced in mid-December 2020 would stop training and racing immediately after an irregular heartbeat led to a myocarditis diagnosis. The Italian was given the green light to resume training the following February, before racing again at mid-April’s GP Miguel Indurain. The 37-year-old now races for XDS Astana after making the switch for the 2025 season.

From a team’s perspective, a broken rider is like a broken wheel: useless. His or her impact is felt by the team, with schedules changed and, depending on the rider, chances of victory diminished. The competitive impact is felt commercially, framed against cycling’s fragile business model. Losing your strongest riders equals fewer wins equals less media exposure equals a struggle to attract sponsors… It’s a domino effect of doom.

Injury has a real and quantifiable impact on a rider’s transfer or contract value, too. The European Sport Management Quarterly, Journal of Sports Economics and Applied Economics have all featured research that shows injury can impact market valuation by 10 to 20%, with that rising to over 30% for a serious or recurrent injury. It’s worse news for older riders, as this can approach 50% for those on the wrong side of 28 years old. Naturally, this drop in market value limits an athlete’s salary and earning potential.

Egan Bernal is a clear example. In 2019, the Colombian won the Tour de France at the age of 22. In January 2022, he signed a lucrative five-year extension with Ineos reportedly worth €2.5 million to €3.0 million annually. Later that month, he suffered over 20 broken bones, a punctured lung and chest trauma after hitting a parked bus at 62km/hr. Since then, though he’s shown glimpses of his past form, he’s not been the same rider. His contract with Netcompany Ineos runs out at the end of this year and, at the time of writing, though there are rumours of either another extension or a move to Movistar, his future remains unclear. What is clear is that his likely next deal will see a salary drop to €2 million or less. Still healthy, but a sizeable percentage drop.

Time off the bike has clear consequences, so the aims are prevention (the ideal) and limitation (the reality). In Fredericks’ analysis, those 1,920 lost days were broken down into 140 incidences of injury and 134 incidences of illness.

When it comes to injury, 68% occurred during racing (compared to 32% in training). That’s significant and even more so when you account for annual workload. While training volume nestles between 18,000 and 23,000km, racing is around 8,500km. All in all, a rider is four times more likely to crash during a race than training.

No one was seriously injured, and all riders started the next day. “That was a positive,” says Fredericks. “But I’m just glad I wasn’t the doctor at that race. He had to dress and undress the injured six riders for up to 12 days, adding an extra two-and-a-half hours to his day. Injury has significant implications for the staff as well as the riders.” (The doctor clearly did a fine job. This was the Grand Tour where Pogačar introduced himself to the world, finishing third and winning three stages in the process.)

Jayco AlUla doctor Luca Pollastre agrees that traumatic injuries are the most common. “While the frequency of crashes is relatively stable, the severity of those crashes is rising, which can mean weeks or even months before an athlete can return to competition,” he says. “We feel this is due to the aggressive nature of racing.”

The most common trauma in Fredericks’ analysis was what he euphemistically termed ‘superficial’, like the road rash Pogačar endured at La Vuelta. Then came damage to bones – fractures or breaks – which shines a spotlight on bone health, a hot topic in professional cycling. Fredericks revealed that a significant number of riders [over 50%] had low bone mineral density, and quite a few of them are actually osteoporotic. Treatment includes bone-strengthening medication, calcium and vitamin D supplementation, and weight-bearing exercise.

“But that raises an important quandary,” says Fredericks. “We want to protect the riders from the risk of a fracture, but will they be interested in running, which we know helps? And will they be happier for more weights if it adds weight? It’s tricky.”

Damage to muscles, tendons and cartilage followed, while in Fallon’s research, hand and head injuries, particularly fractures and concussions, were common, with head injuries the most prevalent for female riders.

Overuse injuries are far less common, says Fredericks, with the majority related to patellar tendinopathy and Achilles tendinopathy, which are the result of the repetitive load of thousands of pedal strokes outpacing the tendons’ ability to recover and adapt.

Arguably, their rarity is credit to bike-fitters, like Phil Cavell, co-founder of Cyclefit in London, who have worked with many professional riders, including the Lidl-Trek team. Cavell’s also an author, whose most recent book, The Cycling Addiction, has just come out.

“To be fair, bike-fitters are only one reference point WorldTour riders are triangulating off,” says Cavell. “There’s also advice from teams and, surprise, surprise, WorldTour trends. Sometimes riders make decisions not wholly based on bike-fit and physio-led opinion.”

Cavell says there are hotspots when working with WorldTour riders, most notably when myriad factors change, like the bike, shoes, saddle and pedals, which can happen if a team’s sponsors change or a rider moves. “That’s when team camps become dawn to dusk affairs,” he says. “There may be adaptations at the foot, knee, hip, back… These adaptations may express over time, so our job is to predict what’s going to happen and put in place mediations.”

“I remember working with a very good rider, recently retired, who started a particular Grand Tour with a 17cm drop from saddle to bars,” he adds. “It worked okay for eight or nine days until it didn’t. We were brought in to revise his drop with a bit more insight and data – saddle pressure-mapping, motion-capture. He could see his issues reflected in our findings.”

Fredericks’ research also focused on the impact of illness, explicitly seen in February 2020 when the UAE Tour was abandoned with two stages remaining due to an outbreak of Covid-19 at the UAE Team Emirates’ hotel in Abu Dhabi. The Emirati team and three other squads were quarantined for two weeks while health authorities carried out tests. Soon after, the team’s lead sprinter, Fernando Gaviria, confirmed that he had contracted coronavirus.

Of the 134 incidences of illness between 2019 and 2021, Fredericks says that 41% of these occurred during racing, with the remaining 59% either in training or between races. “In that time, we had 11 recorded cases of COVID, resulting in a loss of 137 race days [out of 659 lost to illness as a whole]. That’s significant and came down to the minimum 14-day isolation period, plus a graduated return to racing.”

Obviously other teams suffered. Take Simon Yates at Jayco AlUla, who tested positive after stage seven of the 2020 Giro d’Italia, held in October, and withdrew. The Australian outfit’s staff members also tested positive at both the Giro and late August’s Tour de France. The pandemic’s impact is still felt by Jayco, albeit positively.

“We have systems in place that stem from that experience,” says Pollastre. “These range from the use of face masks to strategic room allocation for athletes and the careful assignment of therapists to individual riders, among many other measures.”

“At the beginning of each season, we strongly recommend influenza vaccination for both staff and athletes,” he continues. “During the season, the team doctors hold a weekly call to review the health status of all riders. Relevant information is then shared with coaches and sports directors to support performance-related decisions. Understanding wearable technology data, training loads and providing continuous education are key components in minimising risk.”

Still, despite best practice, it’s hard to avoid SAD (Seasonal Afflicted Danger). “We always expect more issues at the start of the season due to the weather and changes in environment, moving from Australia to the Middle East and then into the European season,” adds Pollastre. “Towards the end of the year, there can also be a spike in illness due to the cumulative fatigue of the season. Although we haven’t analysed it over seasons, at our team I believe that a loss of approximately 10% of training and racing days per rider per year is a realistic average.”

Pollastre says that upper respiratory infections are the biggest cause of time off the bike, which matches both the data from Fallon and Fredericks’ research: “Of the 134 incidence of illness, 60 were respiratory related, like upper respiratory tract infections.” That’s around 45%. Fallon’s study found that racing Grand Tours is associated with a spike, potentially due to “immunosuppression” through the three-week strain. Load management is one method to reduce the chances of falling ill, but that’s clearly more controllable in training than at a race.

Dermatological issues, like saddle sores, were responsible for 18% of lost days, with gastrointestinal issues close behind – ideally not too close behind – at 17%. Interestingly, in Fallon’s research, female athletes report a higher ‘burden’ of gastrointestinal symptoms than the males, although the reasons are not fully understood. suggested that this disparity could be down to hormonal changes affecting gut motility and sensitivity.

Looking ahead, Fredericks is planning to pore over more recent data in search of solutions. What those solutions are is highlighted by Fallon’s research, which ranges from the use of protective clothing, such as Dyneema-enhanced jerseys to help reduce the number of abrasion-type injuries to neck-strengthening exercises, particularly for female riders, to minimise linear and rotational acceleration of the head during a crash.

“Cycling should also embrace technological advances in the use of head-impact accelerometers that feedback to the race doctor’s car to improve care and assessment,” the paper reads.

The problem is that the root causes of injuries and illnesses are multifactorial and somewhat speculative, albeit speculation stemming from education. Cavell gives the example of those traumatic injuries. “Does the trend of a more forward centre-of-mass with narrower bars mean less reaction time if something does happen? And what about shorter cranks? They allow a rider to maintain a deeper drop without blocking the hip, but does this have an effect?” As for the right-side crashing bias mentioned earlier, “That almost certainly has to be correlation, not causation, unless a parcours is especially right-corner-focused.”

Ultimately, for all the sophistication of modern professional cycling, staying healthy may still be its simplest performance advantage. Crashes remain an unavoidable hazard, while illness and overuse quietly erode seasons too. Fredericks’ research shows how much time is lost, but also where gains might come from: better data, smarter load management and preventative care. The marginal gain could be staying upright.

items.title: Lotto-Intermarché youngster announces retirement from racing after just two years in the peloton
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
Lotto-Intermarché youngster Robin Orins has announced his retirement from racing after just two seasons in the professional peloton.

The 24-year-old Belgian turned pro with Lotto-Intermarché last season but missed a large chunk of the year after suffering mental health problems, including panic attacks.

He raced from July to October and took on 27 race days between March and June this season. He announced on Instagram on Thursday that he's decided to retire from racing.

"I’m stepping away from professional cycling," he wrote.

"It’s time to turn a page, filled with emotions, memories and lessons, both positive and negative. A page that shaped me into who I’m today, and one that will be talked about for years to come. It ends earlier than expected, but without regrets."

Orins had excelled as an under-23 rider, claiming second place at the 2024 Liège-Bastogne-Liège U23 as well as two third places at Paris-Roubaix Espoirs, and top-five finishes in the under-23 time trial at the 2024 European and World Championships.

However, Orins struggled upon joining the pro ranks, not making his Lotto-Intermarché debut until the Tour de Wallonie last June.

"The lights just went out. I felt mentally and physically empty. Everything made me tired," Orins said last summer. "I became afraid - of everything, but mostly of myself. I didn’t even have the energy to ride my bike anymore. I lost the joy of cycling."

Last season, he raced Wallonie, the Tour of Britain, and Il Lombardia, among other races. This year, he made his season debut at the GP de Denain and rode several WorldTour races, including Itzulia Basque Country, La Flèche Wallonne, and Liège-Bastogne-Liège.

His most recent outing, and it turns out his final race as a professional, came at the Belgian National Championships in June, where he took part in both the time trial and road race.

"After months of rebuilding myself, I got back on my feet. But I realised how much energy it had taken and how difficult it was to find the old Robin again. No matter how badly I wanted it, the downs were too frequent," Orins wrote.

"This year, I wanted to return happy instead of unhappy. I wanted to enjoy the bike, the people around me, the suffering and, above all, feel fulfilled again. But things didn’t turn out as hoped. No matter how hard I worked, my body said 'no'. Now my head and heart are saying 'no' too."

Orins said his retirement is "like a breath of fresh air", adding that he wants to discover life beyond cycling, which he's done since he was six years old. He did, however, say that his retirement from cycling isn't the end of his sporting ambitions.

"Honestly, this feels like a breath of fresh air. There is more to life than cycling, and I want to discover that with my girlfriend, friends, parents and family.

"Cycling will always have a place in my heart. Every scar, trophy, tear and smile has its story. This is not the end of my sporting ambitions. As my friends say: 'A fox never loses its tricks.'

"Thank you to all the people I love. Cheers! Voske OUT."

items.title: Netcompany Ineos add climbers Markel Beloki and Harold Tejada as Sam Welsford exits after just one season
items.author: Owen Rogers
items.content:
Netcompany Ineos have announced the arrival of two climbing talents, with Markel Beloki and Harold Tejada both joining the team for 2027, signalling a strengthening of the team’s climbing talent in a bid to return to the team's stage race glories of old.

At the same time, the team will lose sprinter Sam Welsford, who is heading for his home squad Jayco-AlUla on a two-year deal.

Rumours of both Beloki’s and Tejada’s arrival have been long-heralded, though the length of their contracts is unknown, with the British team using the phrase "from 2027" in their press releases.

Both will provide much-needed assistance in the mountains as Netcompany Ineos hope to return to the kind of form that saw them win 12 Grand Tours with five riders across 10 seasons, though they have failed to hit the top step in a single three-week race since Egan Bernal’s Giro d’Italia victory in 2021.

Only 21, Beloki is a strong climber with a huge engine, which brought him second place at the 2024 Spanish National Championships at the age of 18. His two professional wins are also indicators of his potential, with his GC success at this year’s Tour de l’Ain coming off the back of a solo move on a mountain stage in the three-day race.

However, Beloki is yet to show his talents in Grand Tours. His results so far are nothing to write home about, as he failed to finish this year’s Vuelta a España, though a steady 35th overall in the Giro is decent for one so young.

“My ambition is to develop as a stage racer and, in time, compete for results in the Grand Tours," Beloki said.

"I know that it takes patience and consistent work, so being able to learn from experienced teammates, contribute to their success and make the most of my own opportunities is something that really motivates me."

At 29, Tejada is already proven, and while he’s not a regular winner, indeed he has just two pro victories; his most recent success came earlier in 2026 when he won a mountainous sixth stage of Paris-Nice.

“Harold is a strong, solid climber with plenty of experience. He’s been consistently up there over the last few years, and he’ll be a great support to our GC riders," said the team’s cirector of racing, Geraint Thomas.

Heading out of Netcompany Ineos’s roster, which currently stands at only 16 confirmed riders for 2027, is Sam Welsford, the Australian sprinter who has spent just one season at the team. 30-year-old Welsford is heading for Jayco-AlUla, where he’s signed for two years.

Clearly talented, his season at Netcompany has not been as rewarding as both he and the team would have hoped, despite starting the season with a stage win at the Tour Down Under. Since then, he’s struggled for results, finishing in the top 10 on only six occasions, arguably not enough for a sprinter.

His departure might also indicate Netcompany’s increased focus on stage racing, where they’ve historically been so successful, and also be a side effect of Dorian Godon’s success in punchy sprints.

As Netcompany Ineos have chased Beloki, Jayco have been after Welsford for some time. "It is really great that we have been able to finalise this deal and have him on our roster for the next two seasons," said the team’s head of performance, Gene Bates.

"Sam is well known to the team staff and riders. We are really looking forward to working with Sam and his abilities on the road. He is really focussing on road racing now and in the sprints. He will add a great deal of motivation to the group, and having him allows us to focus on some big projects for 2027 and 2028."

Welsford has ridden for a number of WorldTour teams since joining DSM in 2022, but sees this move as a homecoming.

"After five years racing at the highest level, it feels like the right time to come home and be part of an Australian team with such a strong history in the sport," he said.

"I’m looking forward to bringing my experience, continuing to develop and, most importantly, racing for something that feels very close to home. I’m really motivated to see what we can achieve together and proud to represent Australia on the world stage."

items.title: A rare return to unpredictability as no Tadej Pogačar at Il Lombardia opens the door to the same anarchy as Worlds – Analysis
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
In the 25 Monument Classics since Tadej Pogačar won his first of cycling's oldest, most prestigious and hardest one-day races at Liège-Bastogne-Liège in 2023, 19 of the victories have been shared only by him and Mathieu van der Poel, with just seven different winners.

The five other champions in that period are far from complete shocks: Remco Evenepoel twice, Wout van Aert, Matej Mohorič, Jasper Philipsen, and Dylan van Baarle.

All more than 230km in length and offering up some of the most attritional routes seen on the cycling calendar, the Monuments have long been where the preeminent riders rise to the top, but even the era immediately preceding the arrival of Pogačar pointed to more of a democracy than the almost total duopoly we've been watching for the past four seasons.

In the 25 Monument Classics before Pogačar sprinted to that maiden title in Liège, there were 22 different winners across Milan-San Remo, Tour of Flanders, Paris-Roubaix, Liège, and Il Lombardia, with only Jakob Fuglsang, Vincenzo Nibali, and Phillipe Gilbert as repeat champions in that time frame, and considerably more riders in play for the wins.

As 2026 nears the final of the five, Il Lombardia, on Saturday, the racing should briefly be returned to the less predictable and – if the World Championships men's road race was anything to go by – almost completely lawless racing largely unseen since the Slovenian has established a vice grip on the majority of major races.

Just as San Remo was for Eddy Merckx, Roubaix was for Roger De Vlaeminck, and Lombardy was for Fausto Coppi, Pogačar has made one of the five his particular playground of choice, and that has been the northern Italian race, matching the latter's record of five victories as he completely destroyed the field 12 months ago to maintain his perfect record.

And anything but the sixth arriving this Autumn, and Italy's greatest rider being overtaken 72 years after he set what seemed like an unbreakable record, would've been one of the shocks of the season, no matter who was on the start list.

But even Pogačar – despite his miraculous ability to avoid major injuries for the large majority of his career – is not invincible, and the most important crash in terms of impact all season, which left him concussed and with a fractured collarbone and vertebrae at the Vuelta a España, has changed the complexion of what likely would've otherwise been another tension-less Il Lombardia.

Throughout his reign of five wins, the Slovenian has only grown more dominant as the years went on, too, winning his first two titles from two-up sprints against Fausto Masnada and Enric Mas – who showed the world exactly how to step into the void left by Pogačar as he soared to the Vuelta a España GC title last month, Spain's first for 12 years.

But the unchanged variable of his perfect record has been UAE controlling the race on the approach to whatever the key climb is on the route, and preventing any of the previous chaos, randomness, and masterclasses at the eleventh hour of the season which long punctuated Lombardias gone by into the 2020s – shown best by the list of former winners – from developing.

In truth, Pogačar is so superior that UAE haven't needed to rely on overly nuanced tactics whether heading to Bergamo or Como, instead just setting a brutal tempo before launching him into the final 30-50km, and to three solo wins at the last three editions – winning by 0:52 in 2023, a massive 3:16 in 2024, and 1:48 last season.

The runner-up in those latter two was Remco Evenepoel (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe), who seems the obvious successor on paper. However, as everyone saw at Worlds in Montreal, where that same theory was tested, the Belgian star is significantly less of a guarantee than his contemporary.

What became clear in Canada is that the gap between Pogačar and the rest is much greater than that of the rest to each other, with Evenepoel likely starting on a par with UAE's leaders Isaac del Toro and World Champion Brandon McNulty, Paul Seixas (Decathlon CMA CGM), Tom Pidcock (Pinarello Q36.5), Giulio Ciccone (Lidl-Trek), and Matteo Jorgenson (Visma-Lease a Bike).

Evenepoel going solo seemed likely before he was brought back down to earth in Canada, and while he can try to just follow the moves and somewhat rely on his sprint, the millimetres and controversial photo finish that saw him snatch the European title from Ciccone's grasp leave cause for nerves to creep in.

Pogačar's brute force approach is what benefitted the Belgian most, particularly last year, with the earlier and earlier opening up of races ruling out anyone from even attempting to beat the UAE rider tactically.

But thinking he can match that as the instigator could prove fatal for Evenepoel and Red Bull's chances, as it's easy to forget what the reigning champion has normalised when it comes to solo attacking, often matching records set by Merckx and Coppi with his daring, but now expected moves.

With that should come what was true of Worlds: a war of attrition being matched by a total tactical battle, where the numbers game may prove as vital as it did for McNulty and the USA en route to rainbows. Evenepoel's greatest asset may end up not being his ability to solo or sprint, but whether Primož Roglič or Giulio Pellizzari can make it into the leading split to add more strings to his attacking bow, and the same can be said of UAE, who are probably still starting with the strongest team.

McNulty and the US showed everyone the blueprint for how to win a Pogačar-less race at Worlds, and it was actually his compatriot Quinn Simmons who came closest to upsetting the usual flow of Lombardy a year ago when he made an all-out assault on the course from the early breakaway.

UAE and Pogačar hoovered him up eventually, of course, and he faded to fourth by the time the race reached the finish, but knowing that the bullet from behind won't be anywhere near as threatening compared to the inevitability of the Slovenian, it could cause the early break to return as a genuine method to victory.

Don't be surprised to see the stars and stripes of Simmons and several others all on the move to try and get ahead of Evenepoel, Del Toro and Seixas, as anticipation becomes genuinely threatening again. However, this would be returning cycling to an even older era if someone were able to pull it off, and the difficulty of the route cannot be sniffed at with 4,845m of elevation gain packed into the 243km.

Mollema in 2019 provides the blueprint

It feels like a lifetime ago that George Bennett was battling away with the Astana duo of Fuglsang and Aleksandr Vlasov until the last 6km of the COVID-19-rescheduled 2020 edition in August of that year, or since Bauke Mollema's well-timed move in the last 20km of the 2019 race saw him emerge victorious ahead of a group of closely matched climbing stars like Roglič, Egan Bernal, and Alejandro Valverde.

What was then an attainable goal for many, Il Lombardia became unwinnable in the years that followed for 99% of the peloton, and the same can largely be said of the other four Monuments. But with the door now open in Pogačar's absence, perhaps the biggest surprise win since Mohorić in San Remo in 2022 is around the corner – and even then San Remo has long stood as the most unpredictable of the five, so that run of predictable winners likely stretches back even further.

Despite their importance in the context of cycling's history and Pogačar's place as an all-time great, the past three editions could have been an email in reality, with everyone, including his rivals, without wanting to admit it, knowing who was going to win barring major incidents.

With the Slovenian returning to action in 2027, it may be the only chance some riders get to win a Monument for the next six years [when his newly-signed contract ends], so they must grasp it with both hands.

Few outcomes would be as compelling as Evenepoel emerging victorious, though, six years on from the horror crash off a bridge which left him seriously injured and leaving the race in an ambulance. But it's hard to see anything but an incredibly complex race play out for the Belgian, so he will have to thrive amid the adversity as he did at the Euros and several races before. If he does succeed, the outpouring of emotion should be cathartic.

Mollema will start Saturday's race as the oldest rider at 39, before his retirement, and it's his method to victory which looks most likely: all the big names together in the last 30km, before someone makes the right opportunistic move, and perhaps that could come from Evenepoel, or Seixas, the youngest man on the start line. This Saturday's race and a return to a more open Il Lombardia won't be one to miss.

items.title: 'I'm here to just go all-out and race without any regret' – Florian Vermeersch prepared for Gravel Worlds title defence
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
Belgian racer Florian Vermeersch is in Australia this weekend, the 27-year-old taking aim to become the first rider to defend the gravel world title since the event was established in 2022.

Now he's in Nannup, Western Australia, for another shot at the UCI Gravel World Championships, where he'll face off against the likes of Keegan Swenson (USA), Mads Würtz Schmidt (Denmark), and Matt Beers (South Africa), among others.

Vermeersch has mostly focussed on the road this season, racing the spring Classics (including podiums at Omloop Het Nieuwsblad and the E3 Saxo Classic plus a top-10 finish at the Tour of Flanders) and the Giro d'Italia. But he's still prepared to defend his title at the Gravel Worlds,

"Unfortunately, I've done only one gravel race. The plan was to do one or two more, but due to my calendar, it was not possible," Vermeersch told this week.

"But I've done a lot of gravel rides at home wearing the jersey, so I've enjoyed that. It was a very nice year, I would say. It's an honour to wear those rainbow colours."

Vermeersch and his UAE Team Emirates-XRG team have planned for him to return to the gravel this week to keep the rainbow stripes in the team along with Brandon McNulty's road world title.

"From December last year, when we were speaking about my calendar with my team, I already got the signal that I could defend my title. They gave me the freedom that if I wanted, I could come here," he said.

"I said immediately that I would like to defend it. So it was a bit of a no-brainer. I didn't really have to fight for it with the team; they allowed me to come, so that's very nice of them and I really appreciate that.

"The last few weeks, to prepare and train for this race, have been very nice. I've made a lot of hours on the bike, and I think I'm in a good place."

The 144km elite men's race route will include 3,713 metres of climbing and much tougher gravel than previous editions in Belgium, Italy, and the Netherlands, with at least 80% gravel on every route, said race director Stephen Gallagher.

"I did the big loop – the 77km loop – yesterday, and it's really tough. I think it's going to be a very demanding race, but I'm in for a challenge, and we'll see," Vermeersch said of the route.

"Some corners were actually pretty sketchy. It's really slippery, and you have to pay attention. But I think now, with the rain coming down, it's going to make it a bit faster and a little bit less slippery in the corners, I think. So for this, the rain is not too bad."

He acknowledged that the route is a major challenge but noted that some pressure is off his shoulders, having already won the world title last time out.

"I think it's going to be on the limit. I'm a big guy, and it's almost 4,000 metres of climbing. But I'm in for a challenge. I really like the course, and we'll see where I end up.

"The good thing is I've already won the jersey once, so this is not an extra stress factor for me. I'm here to just go all-out and race without any regret, I would say. Just leave it all out there."

items.content:
When it comes to the best aero helmets, there are plenty to choose from, but the fastest we've ever tested is the Oakley Velo Mach.

In our in-depth wind tunnel testing of 47 helmets, the Oakley was the absolute fastest aero road helmet, saving up to 8 watts at 40km/h. It was only beaten by a few dedicated TT helmets, making it a serious contender for cyclists who want speed, safety, and cutting-edge design.

It takes it down to just £169, from the usual £280, and a massive £111 saving. In our Oakley Velo Mach review, expert tester Tom Wieckowski scored it an impressive 4.5 out of 5. Along with that aero performance, he reckoned it was also stylish, comfortable, well ventilated, and ticked all the boxes for a top-tier road helmet.

These Oakley deals are showing as limited sizing at Sigma, but there are three colour options to choose from, and the deal is for the MIPS-equipped version.

It's worth noting that in testing, Tom chose a small over his usual medium, which is something to consider if you're pulling the trigger.

It's also cheaper at , but the sizing is even more limited; if they have a size for you, it's an even better price.

The Oakley Velo Mach is the fastest road helmet we've ever tested, and one of the most expensive. This discount takes it down to an incredible price, and if you want to find out why we rated this so highly, then now is the time. It's limited sizing, so you'll have to be quick. Cheaper at Alpine Trek, but not many options to choose from there.

In his review, Tom summed up the Oakley by saying;

"There's not much to dislike, really, and it hasn't given me a second of discomfort or any other issues in months of regular use. If you are shopping for a new performance road helmet, the Velo Mach should at the very least be one of the models you consider."

Highlights for Tom included its ventilation, and with just three front vents, one large main one, and two side vents, which also double as sunglasses storage, it received a big tick there. Tom noted that the large front vent did the job of keeping things nice and cool despite the aero design.

It was also very comfortable; of course, everyone's head is different, but having no hair (sorry Tom!), he added that he's more sensitive to uncomfortable helmet interiors than most. The Oakley delivered a great overall fit with zero issues over numerous hours of testing.

Its aero performance is the real appeal of the Velo Mach, and it has two very cool rubber fins which protrude from either side of the helmet in the back quarter. These 'flow conditioners' are designed to reduce drag and increase airflow attachment, helping the air passing over the helmet's outer shell to stick to it for longer.

It’s a feature that doesn’t appear on many helmets, and it certainly seemed to aid the aero performance in our wind tunnel testing.

items.title: Lidl-Trek announce early departure of Giulio Ciccone on eve of final race together at Il Lombardia
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
Giulio Ciccone will depart Lidl-Trek at the end of the 2026 season, having reached a mutual agreement with the German WorldTour team to part ways before the expiration of his contract, which was due to run until 2029.

It means the Italian will ride his final race for them this Saturday at Il Lombardia, where he will lead the team alongside Quinn Simmons and Juan Ayuso, ending his time after joining from Bardiani in 2019 and managing 10 victories.

"After eight seasons together, the Team and Giulio have reached the mutual decision to part ways, which means Il Lombardia will be the Italian’s final race in Lidl-Trek colours," read a short statement released by the team on Friday.

"We want to thank Giulio for all he has done for the team and wish him all the best for the future."

Ciccone won two stages of the Giro d'Italia, the Clasicá San Sebastián, and five WorldTour races in total with Trek, and wore both the yellow jersey at the Tour de France and the pink jersey at the Giro as race leader during his eight seasons.

Lidl-Trek has undergone major changes this past season, with Italian General Manager Luca Guercilena departing after 16 years of leadership back in June. Andy Schleck has since taken over as CEO, with Grischa Niermann joining as Chief Sporting Officer.

With Ciccone on the way out, Lidl-Trek's climbing core will be made up of Ayuso, Derek Gee-West, Mattias Skjelmose, and new signing Felix Gall in 2027. It also opens up a spot for more new arrivals, with Filippo Ganna being linked with a move away from Netcompany Ineos to Lidl-Trek in recent days by Ciro Scognamiglio at and Daniel Benson's Substack.

If Pinarello Q36.5 is confirmed as his new team, Ciccone would instantly become a main leader alongside Pidcock, who could combine as a deadly duo in the hilly Classics, and as stage hunters or GC options in the Grand Tours.
