items.title: ITA confirms 12-month ban for Kyrylo Tsarenko after three whereabouts failures
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
The International Testing Agency (ITA) have announced that Ukrainian racer Kyrylo Tsarenko has accepted a 12-month suspension from racing after committing an anti-doping rule violation.

Tsarenko was suspended from racing after three instances of late submission of whereabouts filings within a 12-month period.

His period of ineligibility runs from July 1, 2025, to June 30, 2026, and he already resumed racing for Solution Tech-Nippo-Rali back in July. He has since raced the Sibiu Tour, several .2 races in Turkey, and a host of races in Italy, including the Coppa Sabatini, Giro d'Abruzzo, Tre Valli Varesine, and Gran Piemonte.

"The ITA reports that cyclist Kyrylo Tsarenko has agreed to the consequences for his ADRV under Article 2.4 of the UCI Anti-Doping Rules (UCI ADR)," the ITA announced on Thursday.

"Following three instances of late submission of whereabouts filings, which resulted in three filing failures within a 12-month period, the ITA and Kyrylo Tsarenko have reached an agreement on consequences in relation to the ADRV.

"The Rider did not challenge the ADRV and agreed with the consequences proposed by the ITA on behalf of the UCI, namely a one-year period of ineligibility and disqualification of results. Accordingly, the case was resolved via an agreement on consequences."

Tsarenko continued racing to end the 2025 season, taking in 19 race days including the Czech Tour, several Italian one-day races, and the UEC European Championships road race.

However, all of those results have now been wiped out as a result of the year-long suspension, while he was held out of racing for the first half of the 2026 season before returning at the Sibiu Tour, where he finished sixth.

"Considering that the rider was serving a provisional suspension, which he accepted on a voluntary basis pending the proceedings, the rider’s period of ineligibility ended on 30 June 2026. All the rider’s competitive results obtained from 1 July 2025 until 3 December 2025 are disqualified, including forfeiture of medals, points and prizes," the ITA announced.

"No party with a right of appeal has challenged the decision before the Appeals Division of the Court of Arbitration for Sport. The case is therefore final.

"The ITA will not comment further on this case."

items.title: 'They are going to be hard to beat for sure' – Marianne Vos toes the line against a field packed with discipline specialists at the UCI Gravel World Championships
items.author: simone.giuliani@futurenet.com (Simone Giuliani)
items.content:
When Nannup was first announced as a venue for the UCI Gravel World Championships, one rider who immediately looked forward to the 2026 rainbow jersey race in Western Australia was Marianne Vos. It wasn't close to home, far from it, and it wasn't the perfect parcours, but it was definitely somewhere she wanted to be.

While Vos wouldn't go so far as to call herself familiar with the area, she does have history, after coming out for the Margaret River Tour, which swept through the region multiple times around a decade ago. The organising team for that race then shifted focus to SEVEN and, almost as soon as the UCI got into gravel, put up their hands to host a series race and were in the queue for a World Championships.

"I already knew that SEVEN was the event they were doing every year, but being held in May it was always difficult to get here in the road season," Vos told as the event neared. "But as I did also do Gravel Worlds over the last two years, when it fitted my road schedule and when it fitted the team schedule, I was very keen to also do it now."

"When it first got announced, I was already excited back then."

"First, yes, I wanted to go here because it's here," said Vos of the Nannup location for the world title battle. "Next to that, just to get here and try and get to the best level I can, especially after a difficult season. I know winning will be difficult and really hard, but trying my best and getting the best out of the race – that is the goal and the focus."

Vos already knows what it is to win a Gravel World Championships, just one of four elite women in that category, as she claimed the rainbow stripes in 2024 and she also came second to compatriot Lorena Wiebes in 2025.

"If you look at the altitude metres of the race, there's no doubt that it's hard and there's also no doubt that the climbs, although they are not long, add up all the time. In the end it will be a challenge," said Vos.

"I think in gravel it's a combination of physique, a bit of tactics, a bit of technique, and that combination is what I like most about gravel. And, in the end, on this course for sure, the best riders will end up in front. I guess besides mechanicals or crashes, normally the best rider will win, so that's a good thing. It will be a fair and honest race."

Riders like 2024 Unbound winner Rosa Klöser, who won at Sea Otter Europe in the middle of last month, where Vos was third, and this year's Unbound winner Sofia Gomez Villafañe, who has barely been off the top step this year, are among the field heavy in gravel specialists who have been drawn to an event which is expected to open the door for them.

It would, of course, be ridiculous to question Vos' off-road prowess – she has, after all, won eight cyclo-cross world titles to go along with the gravel rainbow jersey – but it's not been her day in and day out in recent times.

"All the disciplines get more and more specialists, so does gravel, and there are some roadies, some mountain bike riders, so it's still a combination of the different disciplines. But for sure, the gravel riders, they are experienced in gravel riding. So in this kind of racing, when it adds up, when you have to constantly be alert on the course, it will be tough competition," said Vos.

"I mean they do this all year and they are going to be hard to beat for sure."

"I think it's an honest course, so in the end, the better riders will end up in front, so tactics can play a role for sure and as a Dutch team, you want to help each other as much as possible," said Vos. "You for sure don't want to be in each other's way. But on this kind of course, I guess in the end it's also about individual qualities. So there is this combination of riding for the country and trying to get the best out of yourself on the day."

'If it was easy then it wouldn't be fun'

Whatever that is, after the race celebrations or commiserations, the prolific world title winner will be taking some time off to reset as she looks forward to a more settled year ahead.

"I'm looking forward to next season, yes for sure," said Vos. "To rest first and to have a proper build-up again ... just getting back to the normal routine and trying to get the best out of yourself."

No matter what that best looks like, in an evolving women's cycling environment where it's getting tougher and tougher to cross the line first.

"It is, but of course, as a team you try and make a plan to get the best result possible, and that's what you work towards. Actually, all these changes in women's cycling and the growth, and also it getting more and more professional, also means you need to adapt and focus and refocus, and in the end just get 100% out of yourself to be competitive," said Vos. "That's maybe the main reason to still also have this extra motivation and spark to go for it because it's never the same and there's so many new races and the competition is tough, and teams have changed."

Vos is now 39, and it is two decades since she won her first elite world titles, but the rider with a lifetime contract at Visma-Lease a Bike's genuine enthusiasm for the sport is showing no signs of waning.

"It's a constant challenge, which keeps it also very exciting and, yeah, it's not easy to win, but if it was easy then it wouldn't be fun. So when things work out – even though sometimes it might take a while, or even though there's also difficulties – that's still pretty exciting. The racing itself is beautiful, and also the training is something I like. I think it's a combination of things that keeps me excited and motivated, and I still have fun."

items.title: Tour of Chongming Island: Lorena Wiebes storms to 21st victory of the season on stage 1
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
The Dutch rider easily moved away from Clara Copponi (Lidl-Trek) and Lara Gillespie (UAE L'IMAD) in the final run to the line at Chongming New City Park on Friday, claiming her 21st victory of the season.

By the time the race reaches its conclusion on Sunday, it's likely Wiebes will have upped that tally to 24, with two more stage wins and the general classification title looking the most likely outcome over flat terrain.

Wiebes has managed the hat-trick of stages before at the Chinese Women's WorldTour event, back in 2019 when she was racing for Parkhotel Valkenburg, where she also won the GC, points, and best young rider's classifications.

SD Worx weren't forced into doing all of the work on the laps around the southern part of the island in Shanghai, but did have to react to a late move from Ruby Roseman-Gannon (Liv AlUla Jayco) in the last 6km.

Everything was brought back before the final 2km, with Lidl-Trek, Jayco, and UAE all taking up the position at the front of the peloton at times, but Wiebes was always lurking with Barbara Guarischi ready to do the final lead-out.

Gillespie had managed to get herself in between Wiebes and her final lead-out rider, but she was jumped by the Dutch rider, who kicked out of her wheel for another dominant victory, the 139th of her already incredible career.

Wiebes is expected to win again on Saturday's stage from Changxing Island Country Park to Chongming New City Park, with another flat 129.4km route on offer.

items.title: Canyon Endurace CF SLX review: One of the fastest and most capable endurance bikes on the market right now
items.author: thomas.wieckowski@futurenet.com (Tom Wieckowski)
items.content:
• $4,200 / $4,499 / $5,999
  • 8.24kg out of the box, incl. storage accessories, tubes and integrated computer mount. (no pedals)
  • DT Swiss ERC 1600 Dicut (35mm)
  • Crystal white / Champagne (pictured) / Atlantic blue

The update and launch of the Canyon Endurace generated a lot of chat in the run-up to Paris-Roubaix.

Canyon split the launch of its latest endurance road bike, launching the top-tier Endurace CFR, which was designed to help Mathieu Van der Poel win Roubaix first, and then announcing the second- and lower-tiered CF SLX, CF, and Allroad models a little later on.

The latest Endurace CFR really looks like an Aeroad, the brand's aero race bike, and has almost identical geometry numbers.

The Endurace CF SLX that you see here has less racy geometry. In fact, Canyon calls it 'an aero bike with all-day fit'.

Canyon sent me the Endurace CF SLX 8 in 'Champagne' colourway to test; it's one click down from the top-level CF SLX 9 and comes in at $4,200 / $4,499 / $5,999 for the Shimano Ultegra, carbon wheel-equipped model.

The Endurace has a slightly cheaper entry price point than the Aeroad, and is a lot less than the top-spec Endurace CFR, but there's not much in it. When do you buy the Endurace, not the Aeroad?

The Endurace has been considered one of the best endurance bikes for a while now, and the bike's latest update saw it get faster and more aero with bigger tyre clearances and slightly more stable geometry.

I've ridden this bike on the road exclusively for several months, and have even stripped it back to race a local hill climb. This bike is at least a must-consider if you are shopping for an endurance bike around this price point.

My size small bike came in at 8.24kg out of the box with a storage bag and accessories, computer mount, TPU tubes and no pedals.

Unless you order the bike with a storage bag and accessories, which aren't included as standard, you can expect it to be a couple of hundred grams lighter than this. It depends on what you might order and fit to the bike, but it's around this mark.

Canyon has changed a fair bit on the Endurace this time around; frame design, geometry and componentry have all changed.

When it comes to the frame, the biggest visual change comes from the altered seat tube and chainstay junction shape. The seat stays are also more aero, and the bike has a new seatpost.

The round S15 VCLS 2.0 flex seatpost has gone, as has the 'Comfort kink' seat tube cutout. The CF SLX now has a comfort aero post in the form of the SP093 VCLS Aero seatpost, which the brand says increases compliance by over 25% compared to a rigid equivalent. CF models will still come with the round VCLS post, which for me offers more comfort.

Fun fact: you can swap in the rigid Canyon equivalent, which is of course what the Alpecin pros like Jasper Philipsen did when they rode the Endurace CFR.

The frame has received aero tweaks and has been to the wind tunnel. The headtube is aero bike-narrow when viewed from the front, and it's clear that aerodynamic performance has been a consideration even on this second-tier model.

Canyon tested this bike in the GST wind tunnel in Germany with a lower leg dummy across a 20-degree yaw angle sweep, with bottles and cages, 65mm DT Swiss wheels with a 29mm Continental Aero 111 tyre up front and a 30mm GP5000 S TR tyre in the rear.

Average system drag at 45km/h for the Aeroad CFR, Endurace CFR, and CF SLX models was as follows:

So, according to Canyon, there are about 5 watts in it. If you're shopping for an endurance bike and are told it's only about 5 watts slower than what a WorldTour pro is riding, I think that's positive news at face value.

This bike also isn't as stiff, which stands to reason. I asked Canyon for some stiffness numbers too for context, and it sent me over some info, in Newton-meters per degree for the head tube (HT), and Newton-metres per milimetre for the bottom bracket (BB); a bigger number in each case being stiffer:

HT: 98,1 Nm/°HT: 114,5 Nm/°

HT: 103 Nm/°

From Canyon's numbers, we can get some context here on what to expect from the CF SLX; it's slightly less stiff in the bottom bracket and softer at the headtube.

I've ridden and raced on an Aeroad CFR, and whilst you can feel the difference, it isn't a gaping chasm. I'll talk about this more, because with this endurance bike getting racier, I want to highlight what you can expect from the CF SLX's riding performance if you are considering one.

What else is new for the CF SLX? Well, the top tube storage hatch has now gone; it's been moved to the down tube. The bits in the tool roll could rattle against the top tube on the old bike; things are silent now, and there's more room. It's a good change.

Tyre clearance has also been boosted to 38mm from 35, providing room for even bigger rubber. My bike came stock with Schwalbe Pro One Evo 32 mm tyres. Starting with 32mm tyres does boost comfort.

The CF SLX can also be fitted with Canyon's Endurace CF SLX Fast Fender set, which comes in at £119.99. The fenders quickly fit to semi-permanent mounts which are fitted to the bike frame. You can of course just fit a clip-on guard, but they tend to need more fiddling with. It's a valuable option if you are considering this model as a winter bike or all-round workhorse, though clearance will be reduced to 35mm with them.

The Canyon Load tool pack costs £19.99 and doesn't come with the bike, so you will need to buy a frame storage bag at the least to take advantage of the built-in storage space.

I'd also recommend just mentally adding £33.99 / $39.95 to the cost of the bike you may be looking at, as you will need to buy the Gear Groove computer mount, which neatly integrates with the handlebars. There isn't really another option apart from O-rings and a basic mount.

Canyon doesn't tend to include mounts or many accesories. It would be nice to see the proprietary mount included with the bike, or just the price increased to cover the mount and eliminate a bolt-on at checkout; it feels a bit clunky to me, especially now that many brands include specific mounts.

The CF SLX 8 comes with a dependable Shimano Ultegra Di2 groupset with a 34-50 chainset and 11-34 cassette. You also get a 4iiii P3+ left-hand crank-based power meter; I found its numbers a tad jumpy compared to some dual-sided PM pedals, but it's nice to get one included for the price.

Endurace bikes now come with shorter cranks; depending on size, bikes have 160, 165 or 170mm cranks, to facilitate more comfortable positions and opening up riders' hip angles. My size small bike came with 165mm cranks.

There's also the integrated CP0048 PACE T-Bar with new 'compact' drops. The Endurace stock handlebar is 390mm to 440mm wide, with three adjustable settings via a pair of T25 Torx bolts under the bar tops. The bars have a 108mm drop and an 8-degree flare.

If you want a narrower handlebar, you will need the Race Drops with their 350 and 400 mm width, but they are going to set you back £219.99. It would be really nice to see these as an alternate option when speccing the bike at checkout.

The CF SLX also gets the Canyon Sport Geometry; the CFR has different Sport Pro geo. Compared to the previous Endurace CF SLX, the chainstays are 3 mm longer, the wheelbase is 16mm longer, and the effective stack and reach are pretty much identical.

The last Endurace CFR I rode was a real hot hatch; this updated model does feel a fraction longer to me, and just a little bit calmer in the handling department.

I've ridden a size small and am 176cm in height; my bike came with 165mm cranks as mentioned, an 80mm stem as standard, and has a stack and reach of 565mm and 386mm. Whilst that 80mm stem size may seem too small, I've ridden endurance bikes with longer stems that felt shorter; the Canyon geometry is well designed to make life easy, whilst still keeping everything looking good.

I think if you're a rider that needs a longer reach, double-check things, but this being an endurance bike, you're possibly on board for shorter reach numbers anyway.

To compare that to the recently launched Trek Domane in a Medium (an equivalent size for me) that I rode, the CF SLX is 10mm taller with a 12mm longer reach.

Compared to a size small Aeroad, the Endurace is 26mm taller and 4mm shorter.

My previous best-ever recorded power for one minute was set riding the Aeroad CFR a couple of years back; I improved on that number in my final week of testing on the Endurace.

Of course that doesn't mean this bike's faster than an Aeroad, but I share that information to show that it's a competitive bike with racy performance. This isn't a boring, endurance machine that can't be ridden hard.

'More speed, Captain' has been my train of thought for harder rides on the Endurace; I personally want a narrower handlebar. Coming from the 35cm Hyper bar I rode on the Winspace M6 left me disappointed at first and has been one of the things that makes the bike feel less quick for me, but I've adapted to the wider bar over time.

I've swapped in the new Dura-Ace C50 wheels I'm testing at times with fast 28mm tyres to sharpen things up, and they do extract more speed from the bike; a quicker pair of wheels does add more speed to the Endurace. Switching back to a 32mm tyre and lower pressures does introduce more comfort and just calms things down, which is great for everyday riding.

If this sounds a bit like you, the Aeroad or even the Endurace CFR (though it's expensive) is probably going to be the model to go for. If you purchase this bike and then constantly look for ways to make it faster, it's probably the wrong choice. Though the prospect of a fully aero, race-spec Endurace with that higher front end is an intriguing one. But if that is the case, the Aeroad or Ultimate, depending on what you need, are the way to go.

However, Canyon has, in my opinion, brought its endurance bikes even closer to its race ones with this update; the differences are finer in many areas. This is a key point to convey: the Endurace is a fast, capable bike with racy characteristics; it's just more comfortable and versatile.

The ride experience from the Endurace has been very good. The handling for me is just a touch calmer and slower than the previous bike, probably due to that longer wheelbase.

Handling and cornering on the bike are excellent; no concerns there for me. Diving into corners or braking hard are tackled with ease. Canyon has created a very capable overall handling package.

The geometry is also very balanced; it's an impressive blend. The bike doesn't feel too short or sit up and beg, but I can still achieve my usual hunkered down on the hoods aero position. However, due to that shorter reach and taller stack, I'm locked into the hoods very comfortably. I can also ride the bike slammed with ease due to that taller front end, and the saddle-to-bar drop makes it look attractive.

It's not as stiff and zippy as an Aeroad, or another full-blown race bike, and that's part of the feeling I miss slightly. It's not electric to ride, but the experience is still very pleasant.

I can't say I feel much ride smoothing from the new VCLS aero post; that's not to say it's not doing its thing, though. I think tyre and pressure will do the heavy lifting for you when it comes to smoothing things out. With a 32mm tyre, or bigger, the ride is refined and smooth.

The shallower DT Swiss wheels are also a good call for me; their 35mm rims just make things that little more user-friendly and aid the handling compared to a deeper, more aero wheelset. It's a nippy yet comfortable wheelset and pairs very nicely with the good-quality 32mm Schwalbe Pro One tyres.

The stock Fizik Aliante R5 isn't a saddle I'm crazy about; the way its profile changes shape, rising near the nose, makes it hard for me to get truly comfortable. I'd probably change it, but as ever with saddles, it will come down to personal preference.

The only niggle I've had from the bike came from the saddle rail adjustment bolt, which worked loose, meaning the saddle dropped forward at very annoying times on a hard ride until I torqued it to spec. Saddle fore-aft and angle adjustment bolts are seperate, which makes life easy, but it's the second Canyon model I've experienced it on, so do check this bolt after a few rides, which you should be doing anyway.

Everything else has been perfect on the bike, and I've had no issues. I feel riders are familiar with Canyon's adjustable stem and bar platform now, and it is very easy to adjust. Just look after it long-term to prevent any issues.

Maintenance and servicing

The key maintenance considerations when it comes to the Endurace CF SLX are front-end related. The integrated Canyon handlebar assembly will need to be looked after long-term to help minimise big workshop labour bills. A full strip-down for headset bearing replacement won't be that cheap.

Minimise front-end blasting when washing, and consider a mudguard or the Canyon fender set for wet weather riding to look after those headset bearings.

Check bolt torque specs every so often, particularly the pair of Torx bolts under each bar top, and the stem bolts.

I'd recommend something like six-monthly-ish headset bearing cleaning and re-greasing just to stay on top of them and prevent them getting into a real state; that's when things will get expensive.

The CF SLX comes in at $4,200 / $4,499 / $5,999 as pictured, a very competitive price for the solid spec, which includes a power meter. Don't forget the £80 / $99 Canyon shipping and packaging fee at checkout.

For me, you get more value with this spec than a range of other big-name endurance bike competitors that I have tested personally.

Don't forget there's also the 105 Di2-equipped bike for slightly less cash, the performance will be on a par with Ultegra overall.

It's a good chunk of cash cheaper than a similarly specced Specialized Roubaix endurance bike, and if you want an equivalent Ultegra Di2-equipped Domane from Trek, you will spend over $1,000 more. Ditto the Cannondale Synapse, which, for a similar Ultegra Di2 spec, costs £6000 / $6,499.

The Ridley Grifn RS endurance bike is another competitor with similar performance, which I rate, but the CF SLX also has it beaten on price by a fair chunk of cash.

The Endurace spec is solid, with no gaping holes or weak points; yes, you might want to change the saddle, and you will need to buy at least the Canyon computer mount.

Canyon's direct-to-consumer pricing has a lot of its big-name competition beaten on price and in performance.

The Endurace CF SLX is an excellent all-round endurance bike that sits at the faster, performance-oriented end of the endurance bike spectrum.

It isn't as stiff or as exciting to ride as a full-blown race bike, but it isn't too far off at all and offers a competitive, comfortable, and confident riding experience that will welcome you pushing it hard and going fast or tackling an all-day adventure.

The taller front end and more relaxed geometry are still purposeful, but it's more user-friendly than the Aeroad or Endurace CFR geometry. If this is a key concern for you, and you don't need a massive amount of reach, don't chance the Aeroad and regret being too stretched out or low; go for the Endurace.

Throw in the 38mm tyre clearance, which gives you plenty of room for bigger comfort-boosting tyres, improved down tube storage and the ability to run full fenders, and you have one of the most well-rounded endurance bikes out there right now.

After months of exclusive riding on the road, I'm in agreement with Canyon's statement that this is 'an aero bike with all-day fit'.

An improved design that boosts aero, clearance and frame storage. A nice looking frame and fork and block colour options. The frame tube shape changes update the bikes looks too.

Very solid, with no real gaps. Ultegra di2 is great, DT Swiss carbon wheels and 32mm Schwalbe tyres and the Canyon finishing kit is all solid. I'm not totally sold on the saddle.

Very good. Not race bike exciting, but this bike can do everything well. Will respond if you are riding hard, but the geo makes it very comfortable. Sure footed handling that's a touch calmer than the pevious model.

8.24kg out of the box with accs. Might just dip inside 8kg without accesories. Not that light, but doesn't create any ride feel issues and there's scope to drop weight.

Very good, a very competitive spec for less money than a lot of competitor endurance bikes on the market with the performance to go with it. There is also a wide range of cheaper models.

items.title: Three course features that could be make or break at the UCI Gravel World Championships in Nannup
items.author: simone.giuliani@futurenet.com (Simone Giuliani)
items.content:
The course for the UCI Gravel World Championships in Nannup, Western Australia, is carved out of a landscape that delivers so many options for a gravel race and the SEVEN UCI Gravel World Series event has, over the years, tried and tested a number of them. The outcome as the organisers now deliver the rainbow jersey race is an unrelenting 144km course for the elite men and a 125.6km route for the elite women.

It will be a test with 3,179 metres of vertical gain for the women and 3,713 metres for the men on what are described as 'Liège–Bastogne–Liège climbs' as the course winds its way through the course in the Blackwood Valley. 'Draining' seems to be the word riders keep using when asked how the course is after they've had a chance to ride it for the first time.

It's the type of route where it's hard to say there are any easy portions, given there is at least 84% gravel, often long undulating plateau sections once a climb is completed and then descents where riders need to keep their wits about them so they don't slip out on the pea gravel corners. Plus it's unrelenting right to the finish.

There are, however some patches which stand out, from sections that could split the field early or create the opportunity for a final winning move, so now it's time to take a closer look at those.

Brockman – First shots fired

This isn't the first climb of the race, that honour goes to Killarney at just over 15km in, but at just 1km long with a 7.6% average the history of SEVEN has shown that it's the climb coming at around 27km into the day of racing that will start to make the difference. It's usually where the first major selection is made.

"You are going to see if you've either got good legs or bad legs on Brockman," said race director Stephen Gallagher.

The 2.4km Brockman ascent has an average gradient of 8.2% and what's more the terrain that comes after is enough for riders to dig in and try to hold on to any advantage that they reap. There is a descent off the top, but not a long one, and then the profile just plots a jagged course for the next 20km, pulling in the climbs of Adina. The real stretch of descending only comes at over the 50km mark, before a flattish section of around 10km that offers some repreive before the climbing begins all over again.

Ellis Creek – The fatigue finder

The climbs continue, and so does the wear and tear which is perhaps why Ellis Creek's 2km, 9.1% average with 169 vertical metres gain hits so hard. The challenging climb that also delivers an extra bit of steepness near the top – comes just after 85k of racing for the men and at around 65km for the women. Plus there is no real relief once you make it over the top.

"I think you've just got fatigue in the legs by that point, so that's why it's the hardest and I think it's deep enough into the race where you can go from there to the finish line," said Tasman Nankervis, the 2023 winner of the elite men's race at SEVEN who also raced this year at the UCI Gravel World Series event which replicated much of the World Championship route.

"The year I won it, I broke away from there," he said referring to the Ellis climb. "It's logical to make a move from there, whereas to make a move from Brockman, that's a bit of a high risk manoeuvre. It can be done, but you can win the race from Ellis, so I think people tend to go more in from there."

The Folly climb is a new introduction for this year, part of the finishing loop which will take the riders close to the start line but then send them off for more, including the 2.4km effort with a 4.8% average gradient that is Folly. It's bound to be packed with spectators, as it is just a short walk from the start/finish line and comes at a point where there is just over 20m of racing remaining.

It starts with riders turning on to a short but relatively steep bitumen section and then it's another turn onto the dirt, which, after a little recent rain is nicely packed down and while there are a few small rocks strewn around and some ruts in some patches they are easily avoidable as it is wide and the main line is smooth.

There is a reprieve part way through the climb which opens up to views of the rolling farmland hills, but then it just kicks in again.

Nankervis warns that this climb isn't one to be taken lightly, with a need to have something in reserve, recounting that in his race at SEVEN this year a puncture had left him behind but he made up around ten positions in this sector as it was one where the lights went out for many.

"It's really hard," added race director Gallagher. "It gets quite steep at the top. You can potentially go solo from that point if you're really strong, or you can certainly reduce a group to one or two riders."

Then before riders hit the line there are still a couple of nasty pinches and the more gradual Lindsay climb on one last descent before the winner of the rainbow jersey is decided.

items.title: Mikayla Harvey and Oliver Bleddyn set to strengthen Jayco-AlUla women’s and men’s rosters for next two years
items.author: Owen Rogers
items.content:
GreenEdge Cycling have announced two additions to their structure, with New Zealander Mikayla Harvey joining the Liv-AlUla-Jayco women’s set up and Australian track star Oliver Bleddyn arriving at the men’s Jayco-AlUla squad.

Both riders have signed with the Australian WorldTour teams on two-year contracts, taking them to the end of 2028.

While Bleddyn is best known as a track rider, where his successes include a gold medal in the Team Pursuit at the Paris Olympic Games, the 24-year-old has plenty of experience on the road. This year, he was second in the time trial at both the Australian and Oceania championships and joined the team as a stagiaire with Jayco-AlUla at the start of August. Since then he completed the Arctic Race of Norway, but has struggled since, finishing only one of seven late-season Italian Classics.

"I’m really excited about what next year can bring. There are some great opportunities ahead and I’m super keen to make the most of them," Belddyn said in a team press release.

"The Tour Down Under would definitely be a special race for me to do. To race at home with this team is an opportunity I’d be really excited about."

The team’s head of performance, Gene Bates, is looking forward to working with Bleddyn, saying, "he has got a huge engine".

"He is a great and enthusiastic young rider and is also gaining a lot of experience on the road, riding as a stagiaire with the team this second half of the 2026 season. We are confident Oliver will be a great addition to the team in many different roles," Bates said.

Harvey arrives after two years at SD Worx-Protime, and similar stints at UAE Team ADQ and Canyon-SRAM already behind the 28-year-old climber. Working mostly as a domestique, Harvey is able to take her leaders deep into hilly finals, and has the engine to bring breakaways back on flat days.

Though she began this year with second place in both the time trial and road race at the New Zealand nationals, she didn’t start her European season until the Ardennes Classics in April. A crash took her out of the Giro d’Italia Women in June, since then she’s struggled to regain consistency, crashing out of the Classic Lorient Agglomération and the Faun Tour Femmes, where she suffered a concussion.

"I am already looking forward to next season," Harvey said. "I am a rider that has experienced a lot, and I feel like I can add this to the team. Alongside this, I am a rider that is not afraid of trying something and being outside my comfort zone. I love attacking and dynamic racing. Especially looking for breakaways and escaping from the peloton."

The team expect her to play a big role in hilly races, including the chance to race for herself.

"Over the past few seasons, she has played an important support role, but with us she will also have the chance to race for her own ambitions again," said Head Sport Director Wim Stroetinga. "We strongly believe she has the talent and ability to be competing at the front of races and fighting for victories, and we are excited to help her take that next step."

Neither men’s nor women’s programmes have been especially active in this summer’s transfer market, Bleddyn joining Will Holmes as the only two signings to the men’s squad so far. At the same time, not only are they about to lose Luka Mezgec and Luke Durbridge to retirement, and Mauro Schmid to Pinarello-Q36.5, a number of other riders are still to announce their futures with the team.

On the women’s side, Harvey is the only new arrival revealed so far, though Erin Boothman has been promoted from the structure’s Continental development team.

items.title: Six-day American Criterium Cup summer schedule confirmed for 2027 while USA CRITS taking shape for spring - North American Roundup
items.author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
items.content:
For a third year, the American Criterium Cup will include six stops across the central and western US to determine overall individual and team champions among well-established criterium events. Races will take place from June 11 to September 5, with Saint Francis Tulsa Tough establishing the first leaderboards in Oklahoma and the finale at the Bommarito Audi West County Gateway Cup in Missouri.

The Tour of America's Dairyland will host the second race in Milwaukee, Wisconsin on June 26, with the third race, the Bailey & Glasser LLP Twilight Criterium in Boise, Idaho on July 10. After the August 1 Fulton Market race with Chicago GRIT, the series swings back to the west for the Salt Lake Criterium in Utah on August 7, and then a month later, the winners will be decided in St. Louis.

The 2027 season marks the seventh for the ACC. Last year each event offered a $16,000 prize purse for pro women and pro men, with the series paying out an additional $44,000 to series winners across several classifications. Plans for any live streaming broadcasts have not been confirmed.

Skylar Schneider dominated the women's competition this year, holding the red leader's jersey from start to finish, while Justin Williams made it a L39ION of Los Angeles sweep in the individual rankings taking the men's top spot. L39ION also won the team titles, the men's team title decided on a tiebreaker against Team Cadence Cyclery p/b Waldo Racing at the final event in St. Louis.

Claudia Marcks (Pedla Racing Division) took the sprint classification across the six races by a single point over Holly Breck (L39ION of Los Angeles), while the men's green jersey as best sprinter went to Owen Gillott (Chaney Windows and Doors Big Shark p/b Pastaria).

USA CRITS, the spring block of one-day races in the southeastern region of the US, will return for an 18th edition in 2027, anchored by the Athens Orthopedic Clinic Twilight in Georgia on Saturday, April 17.

Races in Greenville, Spartanburg, Suwanee and Winston Salem were expected to return following Athens, with additional events still "being nailed down" to bring the series to eight total, according to Gene Dixon, founder of USA CRITS and owner of series producer Swagger LLC.

The bulk of the calendar will focus on races across Georgia, South Carolina and North Carolina, the final calendar set in the coming weeks.

Dixon said the emphasis was to provide a compact 30-day window to simplify travel for riders and teams, especially those traveling from outside the US. A similar prize purse to this year is expected, totalling $200,000 for individual races and overall series classifications with equal payouts among the men's and women's elite riders. All USA CRITS races will provide live streaming, produced by Swagger.

Liza Ray (Kingdom Elite Racing) and Leonel Rodriguez (MC Cycling Team) won the individual titles in 2026.

Next year's Amazon Armed Forces Cycling Classic, June 5-6, will introduce a UCI 1.2-level road race as part of two days of elite men's racing and continue with back-to-back criteriums for elite women. Organisers confirmed that the equal prize purse of more than $30,000 would remain in place.

Last week reported that the UCI calendar had added two new men's races to the 2027 America Tour, Battenkill in New York on May 22 and the Amazon Armed Forces cycling Classic Capitol Cup in Washington, D.C. The long-running AFCC weekend will continue with a full schedule of USA Cycling-sanctioned criteriums, Capitol Cup on Saturday and Clarendon Cup on Sunday.

"This change reflects the vision we share with our partner Amaury Sport Organisation (A.S.O.) for the event's future," said Robert Laybourn, president of Arlington Sports, Inc, and the event race director.

"Every major decision we make is guided by documented metrics and data. The event will continue to evolve and be refined as our budget and other constraints allow, pursuing changes that offer proven value to its growth, success and long-term sustainability."

Organisers at Arlington Sports have not published a schedule yet, however, they have indicated to that the men's course will take place on a 20km (12.5-mile) circuit, the exact distance is yet to be determined. The race is expected follow directly after the early Saturday start of the Challenge Ride, where non-competitive riders have a three-hour window to complete up to five laps of the same circuit.

Then the event will showcase the elite women as the final action of the day, held on the same 1.4km course as last year situated in front of the US Capitol building and the National Mall.

Clarendon Cup events, now in a 29th year, will return to nearby Arlington, Virginia on Sunday. Last year omnium titles for the two days of racing were won by Marlies Mejías (Virginia's Blue Ridge TWENTY28/Deloitte) and Brody McDonald (Modern Adventure Pro Cycling).

items.title: Evenepoel and Del Toro the favourites, but Il Lombardia is wide open – Analysing the contenders
items.author: Patrick Fletcher
items.content:
The final Monument of the 2026 season, Il Lombardia, is upon us and we have a fantastic race in prospect thanks to a fascinating array of contenders, who we're going to delve into right here.

We've been adjusting to a Pogačar-less racing scene in recent weeks, and for all that it's a shame to have the world's biggest star on the sidelines, the racing has undeniably been more open, tactical, and interesting as a result.

That's what we're expecting to see again on Saturday, at a 120th edition of the Race of the Falling Leaves that follows the Bergamo to Como direction on a 239km route with a finale over the Madonna del Ghisallo, San Fermo della Battaglia, and Civiglio climbs.

We arguably have two top favourites – though neither so superior as Pogačar – and a rich array of names who will all feel they have a shot at a Monument on Saturday afternoon.

After winning the European road race title, the Belgian has steadied the ship that listed so dramatically in the World Championship, and as such he starts as one of the top two favourites. As Worlds underlined, Evenepoel is a rider who can blow extremely hot and extremely cold. A one-pitch, know-what-you're-getting Pogačar he is not, but then again, that's part of what makes him such a compelling bike rider.

In a Pogačar-less world, Evenepoel – a former world champion, two-time winner of Liège-Bastogne-Liège and five-time winner of the Clásica San Sebastián – ought to be the next man up. 12 months ago, he soloed to second place behind Pogačar rather convincingly, as he did repeatedly last autumn. But despite bouncing back from that off-day at Worlds, you sense Evenepoel is not quite at the height of his powers.

The Europeans felt like a good example of a race he might have won solo at his peak. Indeed, he had to outsprint Giulio Ciccone for the second time in just a few weeks. Now, Evenepoel's sprint is an underrated weapon that only broadens the way in which he can win these big races, but you can't help but feel that the more we've been impressed by it, the more we've seen it in action, and the less that means he's actually been able to get away.

Even so, he remains one of the very top favourites to finally win a race that he looked like he might have won as a 20-year-old in 2020.

The rainbows may be wrapped around the torso of Brandon McNulty, and while the US rider will have more freedom than if Pogačar were present, it's Isaac del Toro who represents the best shot for UAE Team Emirates and a joint favourite alongside Evenepoel.

Del Toro has all the tools to win this race. As the Tour de France runner-up, he has the climbing legs. As the winner of nearly every late-season Italian classic last year, he knows what he's doing in this punchy part of the world. And as the winner of the GP de Montréal in a sprint, he has the finishing speed to win if he has company.

Del Toro has had a remarkable season in which he has won three WorldTour stage races, finished on the podium of his first Tour de France, and won a WorldTour one-dayer at Montreal. His performance at the World Championships in the same location was widely debated and shot through with allegations, and while we will take his ride at face value, there were tactical question marks that – like we saw at the Giro last year – could do with being ironed out.

But on his day he is just the complete package, an electric racer, and he has a huge opportunity here to take the biggest win of his career so far.

It would be rude not to give the world champion his own section. After all, Brandon McNulty's Worlds win, though highly tactical, was no stroke of fortune. He has largely operated as a domestique, but the immense talent that was evident so early in his career has never been far from the surface, and he had racked up a very respectable palmarès even before the world title.

Since he pulled on that rainbow jersey, he has looked invigorated. Some of it might have something to do with Pogačar's recent absence, but he's been launching attacks left, right, and centre in a sign that the jersey is not weighing him down with any sort of onus of suddenly winning all the time now, but rather giving him a boost of confidence and a spring in his step.

It will be interesting to see how he dovetails with Del Toro. The Mexican might be the standout favourite, but Pogačar is not back yet, and while that's the case there's room for McNulty to go after this race, and perhaps make a bit of a statement over his status in the pecking order at UAE.

The Frenchman takes to Lombardia to round out one of the most extraordinary seasons we've seen in recent years, one in which he rose to the top echelon of the sport and became the most hyped man in professional cycling.

Seixas looks likely to win this race in the future – you could say that about a lot of races – and while it wouldn't be a total shock to see him do it this year, excitement surrounding the recently-turned 20-year-old has dampened somewhat compared to his blistering Spring.

Back then, he was genuinely looking like the second-best rider in the world with runner-up finishes behind Pogačar at Strade Bianche and Liège-Bastogne-Liège, either side of a complete evisceration of the Itzulia Basque Country field. He was fast-tracked into his Tour de France debut, and since then a touch off the gloss has worn off, with a more subdued racing style and a level just a notch lower.

That's no slant on Seixas. Fourth on debut at the Tour de France at 19 is still otherworldly, and he only lost the GP de Montréal in a sprint against Isaac del Toro. But the World Championships, where he cramped in the finale, highlighted some - to be expected - limitations, and also the level of pressure he puts on his own shoulders, berating himself for riding like a schoolkid.

However it lands, and he has all the tools to win it, Lombardia represents the final act of a breakthrough season and the start of a reset that may well lead to a different beast in 2027.

Ciccone has shown his one-day shape is where it needs to be in recent weeks. As at the Europeans, he was out-sprinted only by Evenepoel at the end of the QP de Québec, and he was sixth at Worlds after looking momentarily like he might make his way across to McNulty alongside Tom Pidcock on the final lap.

It's hard to see him winning in an outright sprint against some of the riders on this list, but as shown by the way he took the fight to Evenepoel at Europeans, he has the race craft to make different things happen. When he's in this form and this mood, Ciccone is fantastic to watch. And after the Europeans, he may even be riding with a little extra fire in his belly, which, for a rider who has always ridden on emotion, might just make an all-important difference.

You never quite know what you're going to get with Tom Pidcock, which is probably why he's so exciting to watch. On his day, he's world-class, as evidenced by a palmarès that includes Strade Bianche, Amstel Gold Race, and a Grand Tour podium, along with all his off-road titles.

His challenge to Pogačar at Milan-San Remo this Spring was another reminder of the levels he can reach on his day. But he can also look pretty ordinary, make mistakes, or fade away in big races.

It can be hard to read his form, but it looks pretty good. He had a subdued Tour de France and then won the Mountain Bike Worlds, so it's been a tight one to adjust for a late-season full of hilly one-day races, but he seems to have done a decent job, winning on comeback at the GP Industria & Artigianato and featuring prominently in every race since, with podiums at Tre Valli Varesine and Giro dell'Emilia.

He was also top 10 at the GPs de Québec and Montréal, and in the World Championships, where he was one of the very strongest in the group behind McNulty.

He was also the most generous, and that's probably the most reliable thing about Pidcock – that he'll commit and go all-in for the win rather than playing games and riding for the podium. With no co-leader on his level at Pinarello Q36.5, it leaves him slightly exposed, and he may find himself in awkward situations on Saturday once again. But if he can take that small step towards his sparkling best, then he is well in with a shout of a first Monument title.

Matteo Jorgenson has looked incredibly strong in recent weeks – just a vision of perfect posture and, in contrast to some of the more spritely climbers on this list, pure seated horsepower. The World Championships would indicate that Jorgenson would thrive in a more grinding, attritional affair, but he still had the punch to follow Tom Pidcock's decisive acceleration at Tre Valli Varesine.

The big weakness in Jorgenson's arsenal is his sprint finish. He barely has one. So he'd need to win alone. And that's certainly not out of the question given the lack of Pogačar and given the potential room for tactical manoeuvre.

In that respect, we need to highlight Visma's two-pronged approach, with Davide Piganzoli another credible candidate for the Lombardia title. More on the young Italian in a minute, but what's clear already from the past few races is how well they've combined. Piganzoli, of course, won the Giro dell'Emilia, and much like Brandon McNulty's world title, it was massively aided and abetted by Jorgenson's presence, strength, and actions in the group behind.

The pair both attacked in the finale of Tre Valli Varesine, and this time it was Jorgenson who got to play the finale, but was third in the three-man sprint. Is Jorgenson just the perfect second fiddle, or can he become the main man in Como?

We've mentioned some of Piganzoli's results, and his collaboration with Jorgenson, but the 24-year-old Italian deserves his own slot on this list. He has had a fantastic breakthrough season, shining as the top mountain domestique at the Giro d'Italia won by his teammate Jonas Vingegaard, and finishing eighth himself in the process.

He was then drafted into the Tour de France squad late on, and in truth he was unable to reach his Giro form at any point during the race, but still ended up in 14th place overall. He went on to win the Tour of Luxembourg – his second stage race title of the season after the Route d'Occitanie – before his brilliantly-taken solo victory at the Giro dell'Emilia, which has propelled him up the list of contenders for Il Lombardia.

Are we getting carried away here? I'm not so sure. The 20-year-old Belgian just won his first pro race, at Tre Valli Varesine, outsprinting two riders higher up this list in the process. With that, he has put himself at the forefront of our minds ahead of Il Lombardia.

And yet, he is far from a reliable contender for this race. For starters, it's his first Monument, his first real test in a race as heavy as this in terms of distance and climbing. Secondly, the stunning talent that Widar showed in the U23 ranks has only come through in patches this season (which is absolutely fair enough). Thirdly, Widar is more of a puncheur than a climber, and while the climbs individually suit him, it's far from a given he'll stay the course here.

That said, it was only recently that he was the best of the rest behind Pogačar on a big mountain stage of the Vuelta to Andorra. And when it comes to a sprint, he showed in mid-week that he has one of the best. He may have surprised Pidcock at Tre Valli, but the Briton responded quickly and got nowhere near him.

It could go one of two ways, and while he might fall away completely, you wouldn't count him out of being in podium contention.

Ben Healy hasn't hit the heights he did during his fantastic run of form in 2025, but there have been signs that he's getting back there after a difficult 2026 campaign. The Irishman was 8th at GP de Montreal, 10th at Worlds, sixth at Giro dell'Emilia, and in the main group at Tre Valli Varesine.

He has been an attacking presence throughout. This is Ben Healy, after all, and that's not going to change. The question mark comes over how he uses those bullets. What we've seen in the past few years is a scattergun approach that has often rewarded him but elsewhere has seen him effectively set fire to whole mountains of energy. At Worlds, for example, he launched a big solo attack to reach the front of the race and by the time he'd done so the rest of the group were pretty much back there as well – a long time in the wind when he could have been in the same situation for a lot less money.

But that's what people love about Ben Healy, and if you don't take those risks, you perhaps don't get the rewards. He is capable of a top result here, but needs things to go his way for that magic bullet to land – you can be sure he's going to fire the shots.

Enric Mas did not finish Worlds and was 29th at Giro dell'Emilia, but we're not going to forget about his stunning Vuelta a España performance all that quickly. The Spaniard filled the void left by Pogačar's early exit and dominated the rest of the race with physical and tactical prowess. Mas has had a really bumpy few years, but when it's his day, it really clicks, and he can look like he's on the cusp of those riders in the very top bracket. Just cast your minds back to the 2022 Lombardia – he was the only rider who could get near Pogačar, and he put up a decent fight in the two-way sprint for the title.

So while the past couple of races haven't been anything to write home about, Mas has performed here previously, his form can't have disappeared, and he has absolutely no pressure on his shoulders.

The Italian isn't the biggest star, but he has been operating at a consistently high level for a couple of years now, and he comes into Lombardia with a list of results that reads: 2nd at GP Industria & Artigianato, 3rd at Giro della Toscana, 4th at Coppa Sabatini, 18th at Worlds, 3rd at Europeans, 7th at Tre Valli Varesine. And his one-day record hasn't been far off those levels all year; he has only won one – at Challenge Mallorca – so far (though he did win the Green Mountain stage and the overall at the Tour of Oman).

He probably likes things a little punchier, so the long distance and the climbing load of Lombardia represent an even bigger hurdle to that top step of the podium. But then again, he was eighth and in the second group behind Pogačar at Liège-Bastogne-Liège in the spring.

It's difficult to see Scaroni winning, but he's definitely an outsider for the podium.

We focused on Evenepoel at the top of this piece, and he's definitely the focal point, but Red Bull's team is stacked with riders who might be leaders in other outfits: Florian Lipowitz, Jai Hindley, and Giulio Pellizzari.

We went big on Ciccone earlier, but Lidl-Trek also have Juan Ayuso, who is becoming increasingly inconsistent but has the raw talent to win this race, while Quinn Simmons may find it too climbing-intensive but is sure to show off the Stars and Stripes with an attacking display.

While we're on the subject of strong teams, none are in standout form but are here with Antonio Tiberi, Lenny Martinez, Santiago Buitrago, Pello Bilbao, and Jakob Omrzel.

was a protagonist at Worlds, was third at Giro dell'Emilia, and looks like Netcompany-Ineos best bet here.

also have the small matter of a former Olympic champion in Richard Carapaz.

Tobias Haaland Johannessen leads Uno-X alongside the impressive Anton Charmig.

We've mentioned Widar but is perhaps Lotto-Intermarché's more tried-and-tested top-10 contender.

In Mathys Rondel, Marc Hirschi, and Michael Storer, have a decent set of potential top-10s.

items.title: Egan Bernal says his 'intention is to start the upcoming season' but admits question marks over his future
items.author: Owen Rogers
items.content:
Egan Bernal has stated his intention "to start the upcoming season", but the winner of the 2019 Tour de France has admitted there are question marks surrounding his future.

Bernal posted a personal statement on his social media on Thursday, after the journalist Daniel Benson reported on his Substack that he was weighing up his future, including the possibility of retiring at the end of this year.

Bernal, who confirmed he had ended his 2026 season after the Tour de France, indicated that he will race on into 2027, but his statement was hardly categorical.

"First of all, I am under contract with the team until the end of 2029, and right now, my intention is to start the upcoming season," Bernal wrote, confirming that his season.

Further down his statement, he added: "I don’t know exactly what the coming years hold, and I don’t think I need to know everything right now."

The 29-year-old has been with Netcompany-Ineos since 2018, winning the Tour the following year and the Giro d’Italia in 2021. He has also taken victories at Paris-Nice, the Tour de Suisse and others.

However, a training crash in January 2022, while training at home in Colombia, left him with career-threatening injuries, including a punctured lung, a broken rib and a broken leg, and he was away from racing for eight months. Since returning in August 2022 he has only won four times, three of those in the Colombian national championships. And while he occasionally shows flashes of his old brilliance, he is unable to compete with the current crop of GC stars.

"After so many years dedicated to cycling, I feel I have given the best years of my life to the sport - both as a cyclist and as a person," Bernal wrote.

"I have made sacrifices I never imagined, won races that once seemed like impossible dreams, and experienced both incredible highs and very difficult lows; yet today I can look back with peace of mind, proud of everything I have done and achieved, with no regrets.

"Over time, I have also learned that this sport isn’t just about results, victories, or sacrifices. It is also about enjoying the journey and finding the motivation to keep doing what you love.

"This year, I decided to end my season after the Tour de France. I felt I needed some time for myself - to rest, disconnect a little and regain the sense of calm that can sometimes be lost amidst the relentless pace of competition.

"I have spoken with the team and the people around me, and we are alone the same page: I want to give myself the time and space needed to face what lies ahead with the same conviction and dedication I have always had.

"I don’t know exactly what the coming years hold, and I don’t think I need to know everything right now. For now, I want to enjoy the present, experience this moment calmly, and let time take its course."

items.title: Gran Piemonte: Dorian Godon sprints to victory despite teammate's crash on sketchy final corner
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
Dorian Godon (Netcompany Ineos) stormed to victory from the crash-marred sprint which decided the 110th edition of Gran Piemonte, coming back from being dropped on the final climb in the last 10km to fight for his seventh win in 2026 on Thursday.

Anthon Charmig (Uno-X Mobility) had hit the front in the sprint, but was overtaken by the Frenchman before the line, with Italy's Alberto Bettiol (XDS Astana) taking third.

Isaac del Toro (UAE Team Emirates-XRG) looked as through he was going to power to back-to-back solo victories at the Italian semi-Classic on Thursday, after his UAE team brought back the day's early breakaway and paced hard for the majority of the 185km race, launching him into a first attack 18km from the finish.

The Mexican star dropped everyone on the key La Morra climb in the Langhe hills south of Turin, except for Finn Fisher-Black (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe). Fighting through gritted teeth over the top, Del Toro did briefly leave his companion behind with 13km to go, with the large chasing peloton just 28 seconds in arrears. But on the descent towards Bra, Fisher-Black toiled away to get back on the Mexican's wheel in the final 10km.

They worked together to try and stay ahead, but as Godon's Ineos team and several others contributed to the chase, the two escapees were brought back with 1.5km to go.

As the wind up for a mass sprint started, the twisty roads heading into Bra saw an initial crash with 600 metres to go, and then a second crash around the final, dangerous corner.

Godon's teammate Axel Laurance was the first to hit the deck in the crash that took down several riders, but the Frenchman managed to avoid the incident and deliver the win.

"I didn't have my best feeling, but the team did an amazing job to put me in a good position. Until the last 2km, I just followed Axel and he went super smooth, and I just gave everything after the final turn," said Godon after the finish.

"I was in third position, I went directly and I still had to recover, it was a super hard finish. I'm so happy, one more race in Paris-Tours and then holiday.

Godon has been one of the signings of the season and a huge gem for Ineos, impressing as a versatile puncheur and sprint option.

"I'm still young, 30 years old for me, and I'm on my best years. The team give 100% for me, so I have a lot more chances than other years, and when I have my chance, I think I'm good," he said, adding this title to previous Italian successes at the Giro del Veneto, Coppa Bernocchi, and Gran Premio del Lazio.

"I like it [in Italy], twisty finals, a bit chaotic, and like two minutes all out – I'm better to sprint with an effort before, [because] I'm more of a puncher than a sprinter. In Italy, all the towns are up the top of one hill, so all the finish lines are hard, and I like to race here at the end of the season. I'm happy to have another win here, a famous one."

Gran Piemonte not only signalled the final race before retirement for two Italian stalwarts of the peloton, Damiano Caruso (Bahrain Victorious) and Jacopo Mosca (Lidl-Trek), but it also wrapped up the build up to the final Monument of the season at Il Lombardia, the showpiece event of the Italian Autumn Classics this Saturday.

items.title: Hunt joins the ultra-wide crowd with new 5AM Gravel Limitless race wheels
items.author: Emily Tillett
items.content:
Nothing evidences modern gravel racing as clearly as the cohort of aero gravel wheels that have launched in the past few years.

We've seen ultra-wide aero gravel wheels from the likes of Zipp and Enve, and now British brand Hunt has joined the party with its new 5AM Gravel Limitless wheels, or 5AMG for short.

That extra width isn't just about accommodating bigger tyres. By creating a wider rim profile, the transition between a high-volume tyre and the carbon rim is smoother, helping to reduce aerodynamic drag.

The wheels have been used in racing for a couple of months now, and we've already had them in the wind tunnel as part of our recent CN Labs showdown where we put some of the latest deep-section gravel wheels to the test.

It's well known that wider tyres are well suited to rough terrain, offering greater comfort and control, but their increased size also makes them naturally less aerodynamic. That leaves wheel designers needing to create rims wide enough to accommodate increasingly large gravel tyres while still minimising aerodynamic drag, and without adding too much weight in the process.

So, how has Hunt gone about solving that problem?

According to Hunt, the 5AMG Limitless was designed to balance several competing demands from aerodynamic efficiency and low weight to tyre protection and stability in changing wind conditions.

The result is a wheelset with a deeper, wider front wheel where clean airflow matters more, and a shallower, narrower rear wheel where Hunt has prioritised weight and responsiveness.

The front rim is 54mm deep and 45mm wide, while the rear is 49mm deep and 38mm wide.

Both have a 27mm internal rim width and the brand has optimised the wheels for 45mm and 50mm tyre setups, though they are compatible with 40-60mm hookless tyres.

The more aero a wheelset is, the heavier it tends to be, so keeping the weight down was another priority for Hunt.

There are two build options built around the 'Aero Maximised' rim with the option of carbon or stainless steel spokes. The carbon-spoke version has a claimed weight of 1,317g per pair, while the stainless steel version comes in at 1,447g.

The stainless steel version uses Pillar Super Wing bladed spokes with internal nipples, which Hunt says have been designed to minimise turbulence and make this its most aerodynamic stainless steel spoke and hidden-nipple combination to date.

The 5AMG Limitless Ti_UD carbon spoke version was the lightest wheelset in Hunt's own wind tunnel testing and also recorded the lowest drag.

Hunt has also used its Limitless technology which incorporates a low-density polymer filler in the rim's bead which it says allows them to create a wider rim profile without adding significant weight.

Pinch flat protection was another consideration, with the 5AMG using extra-wide rim beads measuring 9mm at the front and 5.5mm at the rear. This is significantly wider than most wheels on the market, even gravel wheels.

Hunt says the wider beads help 'fend off race-ending pinch flats' while also adding structural strength to the rim profile to protect against rock strikes.

You can pre-order the new 5AMG wheelsets now, with delivery slated for December 1st.

Hunt offers a lifetime crash repair or replacement policy, too.

  • 5AMG Limitless Steel Spoke Wheelset
  • 5AMG Limitless Ti_UD Carbon Spoke Wheelset
  • 5AMG Limitless Ti_UD Carbon Spoke Wheelset (CeramicSpeed Alpha)

items.title: Isaac del Toro reveals mystery knee pain ahead of trying to defend Pogačar's Il Lombardia streak alongside World Champion Brandon McNulty for UAE
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
Despite going without their talisman Tadej Pogačar for the final Monument of the season at Il Lombardia, UAE Team Emirates-XRG will still be starting with one of the strongest lineups, led by new World Champion Brandon McNulty and Mexican star Isaac del Toro.

The latter was fifth on debut last season, while the US rider hasn't raced the Autumn Classic since 2021, when he supported the Slovenian en route to his first of five consecutive wins, matching Fausto Coppi's 72-year-old record just 12 months ago.

With a stacked start list to contend with if they are to maintain the team's run of victories, UAE are also bringing former podium finisher Adam Yates to the start, alongside Jan Christen, Felix Großschartner, Domen Novak, and Pavel Sivakov.

Their main rivals will include Remco Evenepoel, Primož Roglič (both Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe), Tom Pidcock (Pinarello Q36.5), Paul Seixas (Decathlon CMA CGM), Giulio Ciccone (Lidl-Trek), Ben Healy (EF Education-EasyPost), and Matteo Jorgenson (Visma-Lease a Bike).

"We go into Lombardia as defending champions and we’ll have a clear goal to keep that title. The team is very strong and we have many options for victory," said Del Toro on the UAE team's website.

"Obviously Brandon is flying in the rainbows at the moment and personally I’m in good form also. The key will be to have numbers as deep into the race as possible and then play our cards on the road.

"We have a good feeling in the group and understand each other well, so it puts us in a strong position from the start. The rest will depend on the rivals."

Since Worlds, McNulty has brought his rainbow jersey to life with impressive, attacking performances at the Giro dell'Emilia, Coppa Agostoni, and Tre Valli Varesine, finishing 10th, second, and 23rd. And while he had been feeling the effects of his stunning solo win in Montreal, Del Toro's presence makes the opportunistic attack late in the finale just as possible as it was in Canada – but nothing can represent more of a target on one's back than the rainbow jersey itself.

But unfortunately for team boss Mauro Gianetti's men, they have one small issue in the form of an unknown knee problem for Del Toro, which he revealed at the start of Gran Piemonte on Thursday morning. It should become clear after the 185km 1.Pro race whether or not he has been significantly affected, hoping to carry the form which saw him attack Worlds as one of the main aggressors, eventually finishing fifth behind his trade teammate.

"[I'm] good, battling with the jet lag and also the knee pain, but hopefully now we will be OK. So let's see how the legs are, and of course we try to do our best today," Del Toro told CyclingProNet at the start in Asti.

Asked to clarify the knee issues, he said: "[It hurts] a little bit, I don't know why. After the travel, I started to have some troubles – I had the same bike, same shoes, same everything, but I don't know – just let's see how I am and, of course, in the race, hopefully I feel good and can do my job.

"I need to play alongside Johnny [Narváez] and Brandon [McNulty]; they both are flying on these types of parcours. Of course we need to play the cards well, and I need to be alongside them, but we'll see how the race develops and well try to do it."

22-year-old Del Toro extended his contract with UAE earlier this year until the end of 2031, signalling him as the Emirati squad's long-term leader after Pogačar, and after two incredible opening years on cycling's best team, he has only kicked on to bigger and better things in 2026.

He's managed GC victories at the UAE Tour, Tirreno-Adriatico, and the Tour Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes, took third on GC on debut at the Tour de France – while supporting the Slovenian to overall victory, and has won the GP de Montreal. Del Toro is expected to fill Pogačar's shoes when he eventually winds down his career, and he will have an early chance to taste some of that ultimate responsibility this weekend, as long as this knee pain doesn't turn into a bigger issue.

items.title: 'I don’t think it’s my responsibility to finance that' – Gravel pros forced to buy their own kit and fund travel to Australia for World Championships
items.author: Owen Rogers
items.content:
Gravel professionals heading to the Gravel World Championships this weekend have had to pay their own way, while others have had to pay for their own national kit.

The creation of the UCI Gravel World Championships, and the accompanying season-long World Series in 2022, gave the once maverick discipline a more mainstream home, but many national federations are leaving riders unsupported for the first Championships outside Europe, which take place this weekend in Nannup, Western Australia.

With qualification largely coming through finishing positions in World Series events, the national teams are not strictly selected by federations, though the national bodies are able to nominate 10 riders to represent their countries, and national champions receive an automatic entry. However, even those riders selected by their nation are often going unsupported.

Defending men’s world champion Florian Vermeersch, who rides on the road for UAE Team Emirates-XRG, is one of those affected. "It is a trip I have to organise myself. There is no support from the cycling federation." reported the Belgian as saying. "I race there for the national team. I'm just happy that my [road] team gives me the time and space to do this. I get equipment from my team and I pay for the flights myself, but I am willing to make that investment."

understands that not only are British riders having to pay for travel and accommodation, they’re having to pay £60 for a jersey or £120 for a race suit, kit they are required to wear during the race. While that isn’t a fortune, it’s significant given many gravel elites are privateers, especially when they’re paying for their travel and accommodation.

Riding for Ribble Outliers, Sophie Wright counts the British gravel title among her 2026 successes, but has paid for a large proportion of the trip herself, with her race kit on top of that.

"I think it's a bit odd for us to have to buy our own kit from our national federation to represent our country. Especially as an elite professional rider, British champion, it would be nice for BC to offer some level of support," she told .

Compatriot Maddy Nutt has ridden every edition of the Gravel Worlds to date and is a pure privateer, funding the trip to Western Australia from the sponsorship money she lives off.

"What if someone did podium and they were in the wrong kit, it wouldn’t look great for British Cycling and their sponsors. I think they’d even be at risk of disqualification, but at the same time, should it then be the athletes’ responsibility to pay for kit in order to prevent any poor reflection on BC?

"I could wear kit from two years ago, but then in the photos on my social media I won’t be wearing the correct GB kit. I think it’s important that I’m in the right kit, but I don't think it's my responsibility to finance that."

"Part of the reason I am not going is because of the conflicting races, but another part is the cost to go to Australia," said US gravel champion Cobe Freeburn. "It would have been very expensive and I would not have gotten any support from either USA Cycling or from Trek. I'm not surprised that only three US men are making the trip with the conflicting dates and the lack of support."

In Marianne Vos and Geerike Schreurs, the Dutch have two contenders for the title and are sending staff to support them, but while they are providing their riders with accommodation, they have to pay their own way to Australia, though Schreurs will be travelling with her Specialized Off-Road trade team.

"We get really good support from Specialized Off-Road, so for us riders it's actually just like normal travel to a race. So it's pretty easy," she said. However, while clothing isn’t the issue it is for the British riders, the Dutch federation is providing used kit.

"They provide the clothing, but you have to give it back afterwards, then they use it for the next thing. So I try not to think about it too much that someone else has been wearing that kit!"

The Australian, Belgian and British federations all make a distinction between Olympic and non-Olympic disciplines when providing support to riders attending World Championships, explaining the lack of support for their elite riders.

"As a non-Olympic discipline, the funding and resources available to support gravel differ from those available in some other areas of the sport," a British Cycling spokesperson told . "We remain committed to supporting the growth of gravel and will continue to explore the opportunities and resources available to support future editions of the event as the discipline develops."

For their part, USA Cycling’s Selection Criteria document makes it clear there is no support: "FINANCIAL RESPONSIBILITY - Athletes who receive automatic invitations from the UCI or are nominated by the USA Cycling Athlete Discretionary Selection procedures are responsible for their own expense associated with this event. USA Cycling will not assume financial responsibility for any athletes."

items.title: Movistar poach top under-23 talent from UAE Team Emirates-XRG
items.author: Matilda Price
items.content:
UAE Team Emirates-XRG are set to lose one of their emerging young talents in 2027, with Gen Z rider Mateo Ramírez exiting the team to turn pro with Movistar.

Ramírez, 20, from Ecuador, finished fourth overall at the Tour de l'Avenir this summer, just a few weeks after taking the runner-up spot at the Giro d'Italia Next Gen, and has established himself as one of the most exciting GC talents in the under-23 peloton.

His contract with UAE Team Emirates-XRG Gen Z only ran to the end of this year, though, and with their WorldTour squad nearly full for 2027, there did not seem to be space for him to turn pro this winter. So instead of spending another year with the under-23 team, Ramírez found a pro contract with Movistar.

"I'm very happy and excited to start my WorldTour career with Movistar. It's a team with a huge history in cycling and I think it's a great fit for me, where I feel I can continue to grow, develop as a rider and gain experience," he said.

"I am very motivated for next year and I want to give my best, continue evolving every day and make the most of this opportunity to achieve the desired goals."

Still only 20, Ramírez has already shown where his abilities lie as a top-level climber and GC specialist, and while Movistar never lack climbers, they haven't always had a serious GC contender on their books.

After Enric Mas' victory at the Vuelta a España, their stock as a proper GC team has only risen, though, and Ramírez will join the likes of Cian Uijtdebroeks and Iván Romeo as their next generation of overall contenders.

Ramírez is already the team's fifth signing for 2027, and he will join compatriot Jefferson Cepeda at what is set to be a strong Movistar squad for the coming seasons.

"Mateo is a very talented rider with great potential for improvement," team manager Sebastián Unzue said.

"Our goal is to support him every step of the way in his development so that he reaches his full potential in the coming years. We are very excited about his arrival and eager to start working together."

A rare 'loss' for UAE Team Emirates-XRG

While we don't know the ins and outs of Ramírez's negotiations with UAE, and how much they wanted to keep him on their books, it's unusual to see a young talent exiting their ranks when their potential is still developing.

The team have a habit of identifying and locking in talent long-term. However, this move perhaps highlights the limitations of that: even when you have the budget to sign whoever you like, you're still constrained by roster space, and even the Goliaths of the peloton can't just sign everyone.

From Ramírez's side, he clearly feels ready to turn professional, and in the current era, making that step up at 20 is hardly unusual, so you can see why he sought a WorldTour contract rather than opting to spend another year at under-23 level.

So while it may be an unusual tale, a young climber leaving UAE, it's a good thing to see talent spreading around the peloton. After Movistar's exploits this year at the Vuelta a España, it's exciting for them to have a future GC contender on their books.
